shortlist.title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
shortlist.abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

shortlist.title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
shortlist.abstract: The ability to observe the social behaviour of others and use observed information to bias future action is a fundamental building block of social cognition1–3. Aggression observation activates hypothalamic neurons relevant for aggression control4,5, but whether observation and experience engage common circuit mechanisms that promote a new shared behavioural policy is unclear. Here we develop a strategy to perform large-scale cell-type-specific recordings across subcortical networks for social behaviour generation and learning. We record longitudinally while animals train through direct aggression experience or observation, then probe shared differences in behaviour and neural activity in a novel aggression context. After training, we detect unique signatures of a shared adaptive behavioural strategy that is absent in animals without training. During aggression observation, observed behaviour recruits widespread activation across subcortical networks for behavioural generation and mimics activity evoked by experienced behaviour, and shared neural changes persist into the novel aggression context. Multiregion modelling reveals shared changes to a core aggression network across both experience and observation, including a widespread reduction in inhibition, which we find is necessary for adaptive behavioural change. Together, this demonstrates that experience-like activity during aggression observation can recruit a shared inhibitory plasticity mechanism that biases behaviour toward adaptive proactive behavioural strategies. Aggression experience and observation recruit a brain-wide network of excitatory, inhibitory and valence signals, and changes to this activation pattern predict a shared adaptive behaviour-control policy in a new aggression context.

shortlist.title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
shortlist.abstract: RNA language models have achieved strong performances across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by its hierarchical structure, making the integration of structural information into pre-training essential. Existing methods often depend on noisy structural annotations or introduce task-specific biases, limiting model generalizability. Here, we introduce structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model that is pre-trained on millions of RNA sequences and secondary structures data by integrating base pairing interactions into masked language modeling through a novel pair matching operation. The structure-guided mask and nucleotide-level mask are further balanced by a dynamic masking ratio. structRFM learns joint knowledge of sequential and structural data, producing versatile representations, including classification-level, sequence-level, and pairwise matrix features, that support a broad spectrum of downstream adaptations. structRFM ranks among the top models in zero-shot homology classification across fifteen biological language models, and sets new benchmarks for secondary structure prediction. structRFM further derives Zfold, which enables robust and reliable tertiary structure prediction, with consistent improvements in estimating 3D structures and their accordingly extracted 2D structures, achieving a pronounced 19% performance gain compared with AlphaFold3 on RNA Puzzles dataset. In functional tasks such as internal ribosome entry site identification, structRFM achieves a whopping 49% performance gain in F1 score. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight a promising direction for developing multi-modal RNA language models in…

shortlist.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
shortlist.abstract: Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour 1–5 . However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

shortlist.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
shortlist.abstract: Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age 1–3 . How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested 4 , with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce ) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp ), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp ), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts 5–8 . Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory 9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

shortlist.title: Shock Breakout from Mildly Relativistic Ejecta in a Dense Wind: The Case of EP260321a/SN 2026gzf
shortlist.abstract: We present shock breakout (SBO) modeling of the recently discovered X-ray transient EP260321a detected by the Einstein Probe mission. Our semianalytic model, based on our previous work, follows the interaction between a supernova ejecta with a mildly relativistic outer envelope and a dense, wind-like circumstellar medium (CSM) by using a thin-shell approximation that incorporates relativistic effects. We find that the observed properties of the X-ray emission are well explained by the breakout emission powered by a high-velocity envelope with a kinetic energy of ∼3.5 × 10 49 erg (excluding the supernova ejecta) and a dense wind characterized by a mass-loss rate of M ̇ ≃ 1.2 × 1 0 − 3 ( v w / 1 0 3 km s − 1 ) M ⊙ yr − 1 , where v w is the wind velocity. The observed burst duration requires the dense CSM to extend up to ∼350 R ⊙ , corresponding to a CSM mass of ∼10 −5 M ⊙ . These results demonstrate that SBO observations provide a sensitive probe of mass loss from stripped-envelope supernova progenitors shortly before core collapse.

shortlist.title: Exorcising ghosts with gravitational waves
shortlist.abstract: General Relativity (GR) is an effective field theory valid in the infrared regime. Quadratic curvature extensions intended to probe ultraviolet physics generically propagate a massive spin-2 ghost and are therefore non-unitary. One route to remove ghost is by enlarging the geometric sector (torsion, non-metricity). We investigate the infrared phenomenology of both the standard (ghostful) and ghost-free fourth-order gravity theories by computing Gravitational Wave (GW) emission and confronting the results with observations such as the orbital-period decay of quasi-stable binaries such as PSR B1913+16 and PSR J1738+0333 and the chirp-mass evolution of GW170817. In the ghostful theory, besides the theoretical inconsistency due to non-unitarity, there are also phenomenological problems: the massless spin-2 GW flux cancels the combined GW fluxes of the massive spin-2 ghost and massive spin-0 scalar in the vanishing-mass limit, so the GR quadrupole formula is not recovered at the leading order. As a result, we obtain the GW constraint on the ghostful theory as m 10⁻¹¹ eV, where m is the mass of the massive modes. By contrast, the ghost-free theory smoothly reproduces the Newtonian potential and GR quadrupole formulae when the two coupling constants α₁ and α₂ vanish, independently of the mass m. Therefore, GW observations put mass-dependent upper bounds on the size of the coupling constants. For example, if we assume α₁≃α₂ for simplicity, then we obtain α_(1,2) 4.2× 10⁸³ for m 3× 10⁻¹⁶ eV and α_(1,2) 1.3× 10⁷⁵ for m 10⁻¹¹ eV. To our knowledge, these are the first astrophysical-scale bounds reported for ghostful and ghost-free fourth-order gravity.

shortlist.title: Sound propagation in striped supersolid gases at zero temperature
shortlist.abstract: The role of dimensionality in the identification of sound modes in many-body systems characterized by the spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry is a topic of high interdisciplinary interest in both classical and quantum systems. The emergence of stripes in superfluids is a particularly interesting example where the dimensionality of the system differs from the one of the crystal phase. Here we present a unified hydrodynamic approach for the sound propagation in the stripe phase realized in ultracold dipolar and spin-orbit-coupled Bose gases at zero temperature. Despite the deep difference of the two platforms at a microscopic level, a similar hydrodynamic description can be formulated at a macroscopic level. The main difference between the two platforms is the lack of Galilean invariance in the spin-orbit case, resulting in a different identification of the normal (non-superfluid) component of the density. In both cases the spectrum comprises two sounds, reflecting the spontaneous breaking of the U(1) and translational symmetries. Both sounds exhibit an anisotropic behavior. A comparison with the first and second sounds of the smectic-A liquid crystal is also presented.

shortlist.title: Gate-based readout and cooling of neutral atoms
shortlist.abstract: Neutral atom arrays have seen tremendous progress in quantum simulation, quantum metrology, and fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, hardware constraints such as atom loss and heating remain significant challenges. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive ancilla-based toolbox for optical tweezer experiments that utilizes high-fidelity Rydberg entangling gates and ancilla atoms to mitigate these physical limitations. First, we demonstrate repeated ancilla-based atom readout, achieving improved detection fidelity over multiple rounds with minimal perturbation to data atoms. Second, leveraging the quantized motional states in tweezer-trapped strontium atoms, we transduce quantum information from the electronic to the motional manifold. This enables us to perform mid-circuit ancilla-based atom loss detection in a coherence-preserving fashion. Finally, we demonstrate algorithmic cooling, a circuit-based sequence that deterministically cools data atoms by transferring their motional entropy to the electronic states of ancilla atoms. We observe a marked reduction in the atomic temperature of data atoms. These tools offer a pathway to continuous operation in tweezer clocks and complement recent developments in continuous reloading experiments.

shortlist.title: The Deep Newtonian Regime in Late-time Blast Waves: Inevitable Transition and Distinct Flux Signatures
shortlist.abstract: In many astrophysical transients, outflows drive shocks into the ambient medium, accelerating electrons to nonthermal energy distributions that produce broadband synchrotron emission. At late times, even initially collimated relativistic jets evolve into quasi-spherical Newtonian blast waves. As the shock decelerates, the post-shock internal energy per particle decreases; below a critical velocity β DN ≈ 0.2 , only a fraction ξ e < 1 of electrons are accelerated to relativistic energies, defining the deep Newtonian (DN) regime. We develop a unified analytic framework for synchrotron emission in this phase, applicable to both single-velocity and stratified ejecta. For gamma-ray burst afterglows in a uniform medium, the DN transition occurs at t DN ≈ 3.7 E 51 1 / 3 n 0 − 1 / 3 yr, yielding a shallower decay by δα = 6( p − 2)/5 relative to standard Newtonian predictions. For kilonova remnants ( E 0 = 10 50.5 erg, M ej = 0.1 M ⊙ ), the DN phase begins prior to deceleration; neglecting it underestimates radio flux by factors of ∼3–5 during coasting and even more thereafter. Magnetar-boosted remnants ( E ∼ 10 52 erg) should reach ∼ 10 – 100 μ Jy at 3 GHz at ∼ 40Mpc, though limits on GW170817 already disfavor a long-lived millisecond magnetar. In core-collapse supernovae in a wind medium ( ρ ∝ r − k ), the peak luminosity remains constant during coasting, while ν pk ∝ t −1 ; for SN 2023ixf, we find k = 1.29 ± 0.14. The DN spectral energy distribution typically satisfies ν m < ν sa < ν c , peaking at sub-GHz frequencies where LOFAR and SKA-low are most sensitive. Even nondetections place robust constraints on ambient density and outflow energetics.

shortlist.title: ATLAS. III. Dust around Little Red Dots: Hydrogen Line Ratios beyond Dust-free Non-Case B Models
shortlist.abstract: We investigate broad hydrogen line ratios in little red dots (LRDs) using five high-redshift ( z > 2) sources from James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) medium/high-resolution spectra in the DAWN JWST Archive (DJA) and 15 low-redshift sources ( z = 0.1–0.9) from the literature, all with broad H β detected at >5 σ . After carefully measuring the broad-line fluxes while accounting for absorption features and neighboring emission lines, we find that the broad H α /H β ratios are very high, ranging from 6 to 30, well above the Case B recombination value. Using plane-parallel C loudy photoionization models with the total line emission from both sides of the slab, we investigate the physical origin of the broad hydrogen line ratios beyond Case B, jointly modeling the Balmer and Paschen line ratios for the subset of one high- z and two low- z LRDs with detected broad Paschen lines. We find that one low- z LRD is reproduced by a high gas number density ( log ( n H / cm − 3 ) ∼ 10 –11) on the broad-line H α /H β –Pa β /Pa γ plane, whereas the remaining two LRDs additionally require substantial dust extinction of E ( B − V ) ≳ 0.2, even after accounting for non-Case B effects. Since the narrow H α /H β ratios do not indicate such large dust extinction, these results demonstrate that the obscuring dust is spatially associated with the broad-line region. Even without Paschen-line measurements, two and eight LRDs in the high- and low-redshift samples, respectively, exhibit H α /H β > 13, which cannot be reproduced by the non-Case B models, suggesting that dust obscuration might be common among LRDs, occurring in at least about half of the population. Such dust may represent a lower-column-density counterpart of the dusty torus in active galactic…

shortlist.title: S = 1 pyrochlore magnets with competing anisotropies: A tale of two Coulomb phases, Z 2 flux confinement, and XY-like transitions
shortlist.abstract: We argue that the low-temperature physics of S=1 pyrochlore magnets with a predominantly Ising-like easy-axis exchange coupling J that favors the local tetrahedral body diagonals, and a comparably large easy-plane single-ion anisotropy Δ=J + μ (|μ| J) that favors the plane perpendicular to these local axes will exhibit interesting new phenomena due to the competition between J and Δ. In the T/J → 0 limit, we find three low temperature phases as a function of μ/T: a short-range correlated paramagnetic phase, and two topologically-distinct Coulomb liquids separated by a Z₂ flux confinement transition. Both Coulomb liquids are described at long-wavelengths by a fluctuating divergence-free polarization field and have characteristic pinch-point singularities in their structure factor. In one Coulomb phase, the flux of this polarization field is confined to {\em even} integers, while it takes on all integer values in the other Coulomb phase. Experimental realizations with |μ| J and negative are predicted to exhibit signatures of a transition from a flux-deconfined Coulomb phase to the flux-confined Coulomb phase as they are cooled below T_(c₂) ≈ 1.57|μ|, while realizations with positive μ J will show signatures of a transition from a flux-deconfined Coulomb liquid to a short-range correlated paramagnet via a continuous XY-like transition at T_(c₁) ≈ 0.98 μ.

shortlist.title: Unveiling Multimessenger Emission from Hidden Cores of Microquasars
shortlist.abstract: Microquasars are radio-emitting X-ray binaries with relativistic jets and are established sources of ∼100 TeV gamma rays, making them promising candidates for cosmic-ray acceleration. Motivated by recent detections of ∼100 TeV photons from Cygnus X-1 and multi-PeV photons from Cygnus X-3, we employ the Astrophysical Multimessenger Emission Simulator (AMES) to model their multimessenger emission from radio to ultrahigh-energy gamma rays. Our modeling suggests that particle acceleration is extremely efficient in the jet region. The observed ≳0.1 PeV gamma rays can originate from either pγ or pp interactions, depending on the location and physical conditions of the emission region, while also reproducing the lower-energy spectra. These configurations yield observationally testable predictions. In the poorly constrained 0.1–10 TeV band, the models predict either a deep valley, a mild suppression, or a power-law spectrum. Additionally, models involving compact emission regions comparable to the orbital separation predict strong variability, while those invoking more extended and static external zones show more stable behavior. We also provide a possible qualitative explanation for the energy-dependent modulation patterns, relying primarily on changes in the Doppler factor and external γγ absorption. In particular, explaining the PeV emission from Cygnus X-3 favors a compact emission region, for which a magnetic field strength of order 10 2 G is required. Finally, after accounting for pion and muon cooling, the predicted neutrino flux is suppressed, implying that detection is more challenging than previously thought.

shortlist.title: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
shortlist.abstract: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Twist angle, pressure, and strain directly modify the lattice and thus act as highly effective tuning parameters. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. In selected doping regimes, the elastoresistance exhibited a Curie-Weiss-like temperature divergence. We discuss possible microscopic origins, including nematic fluctuations and enhanced electronic entropy from fluctuating isospin moments. Our work establishes uniaxial strain as a versatile probe of correlated physics in a moiré material.

shortlist.title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
shortlist.abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Large language models show that language is learnable from data, but their scale and training conditions differ sharply from a child’s natural experience. We trained cognitively feasible, child-specific models on longitudinal home recordings from eight children across their first 1000 days of life. Each model learned incrementally from a single child’s ordered speech input without prior linguistic knowledge, developing phoneme-like and word-form representations that tracked each child’s learning pace. Learning was dependent on dense daily sampling and replay of recent input, indicating that both experience- and memory-related processes are necessary. These findings show that everyday experience contains sufficient structure for language learning and establish child-specific modeling for testing developmental theories.

shortlist.title: Early epidemiological and spatial assessment of the Bundibugyo virus outbreak 2026
shortlist.abstract: A Bundibugyo virus outbreak was first reported on May 15th, 2026 in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with multiple cases reported across health zones during the early phase of the outbreak and suggestions of circulation weeks prior to detection. We pair highly resolved case and testing records with human mobility data to investigate the early outbreak dynamics of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). We show that human movement was a principle driver of early spatial expansion between May 10th and June 1st when the number of health zones and health areas reporting positive cases increased by 12 and 49, respectively. The early doubling time was estimated at ~10 days. Our work shows the rapid spatial expansion and growth of BVD with implications for intervention strategies.

shortlist.title: Design and Evolution of an Orthogonal HaloTag for Multiplexed Labeling in Cells
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: The self-labeling protein HaloTag is used to install a wide variety of functional small molecules in cells and living organisms with exquisite specificity with respect to cell type and subcellular localization. HaloTag is a core part of many biotechnology-based tools for sensing, tracking, and manipulating biological systems with a high degree of spatial and temporal control. Due to the limitations of fluorescent proteins and other self-labeling proteins, most of these tools have historically been restricted to a single channel. In this work, we used structure-guided rational design and directed evolution to produce an orthogonal HaloTag protein called OrthoTag which reacts selectively with a modified chloroalkane substrate. OrthoTag retains many of HaloTag’s superior properties, and reaction rate measurements with purified proteins show OrthoTag and its substrate have 109-fold mutual orthogonality to HaloTag with respect to substrate concentration. We demonstrate the application of OrthoTag for multiplexed labeling experiments in mammalian cells with minimal optimization. Going forward, OrthoTag should be straightforward to incorporate into HaloTag-based systems to allow simultaneous measurement or manipulation of two biological targets or processes. The availability of multiple high-performance self-labeling proteins will enable the continued development of new multiplexed biotechnology methods.

shortlist.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
shortlist.abstract: BACKGROUND: In patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can be performed to establish reperfusion. Data comparing prehospital ECPR with conventional care regarding survival until hospital discharge among patients who are 50 years of age or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest are limited. METHODS: In a nationwide, nonrandomized study conducted in the Netherlands, we evaluated the outcomes in young adults who were attended by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) that were equipped to deliver prehospital ECPR (intervention group) as compared with those attended by HEMS without ECPR capability (conventional group). The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge. RESULTS: A total of 144 patients were included in the intervention group, and 87 were included in the conventional group. In the intervention group, 57 of 144 patients (40%) survived until hospital discharge, as compared with 17 of 87 patients (20%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 2.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.59 to 4.66; P = 0.002). At 6 months, a favorable neurologic outcome was reported in 51 of 141 patients (36%) in the intervention group and in 11 of 85 patients (13%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 4.22; 95% CI, 2.82 to 6.32). There were 32 adverse events in the intervention group and 11 in the conventional group. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients who were 50 years of age or younger with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, incorporating ECPR into HEMS was associated with improved survival until hospital discharge, as compared with conventional care. shortlist.title: Intismeran Autogene plus Pembrolizumab for Resected Stage IIB to IV Melanoma
shortlist.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intismeran autogene (intismeran) is an individualized neoantigen therapy that is designed to induce new T-cell responses and expand preexisting T-cell responses against patient-specific tumor neoantigens, which may potentially improve the efficacy of adjuvant therapy in patients with melanoma. METHODS: In this phase 3, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned patients with completely resected stage IIB to IV cutaneous melanoma in a 2:1 ratio to receive intramuscular intismeran (at a dose of 1 mg) or placebo every 3 weeks for nine doses; all the patients received intravenous pembrolizumab (at a dose of 400 mg) every 6 weeks for nine cycles. The primary end point was investigator-determined recurrence-free survival, assessed in a time-to-event analysis. Key secondary end points included investigator-determined distant-metastasis-free survival (assessed in a time-to-event analysis) and safety. RESULTS: A total of 1137 patients underwent randomization: 757 to the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 380 to the placebo-pembrolizumab group. The median follow-up was 24.6 months. Recurrence-free survival at 24 months was 82.2% in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 70.0% in the placebo-pembrolizumab group (two-sided P<0.001); the piecewise hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 1.49) before 6 months and 0.42 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.58) after 6 months. Distant-metastasis-free survival at 24 months was 88.5% with intismeran-pembrolizumab and 80.2% with placebo-pembrolizumab (two-sided P = 0.002); the piecewise hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% CI, 0.58 to 1.79) before 6 months and 0.50 (95% CI, 0.34 to 0.73) after 6 months. shortlist.title: Named Reactions under Mechanochemical Conditions: A Critical Survey
shortlist.abstract: Mechanochemistry has progressed from a niche interest to a core method for solvent-free synthesis, providing sustainable and mechanistically unique alternatives to traditional solution-based chemistry. When controlled impact, shear, or vibrational energy is applied under solvent-free or solvent-lean conditions, reactions are promoted within dynamically renewed interfacial regions, revealing new patterns of selectivity, energy efficiency, and process design. This review surveys the historical development, fundamental principles, and analytical frameworks of mechanochemistry, together with an extensive compilation of named organic reactions conducted under mechanochemical conditions. By comparing mechanochemical reactions with their solution-phase counterparts, this review clarifies how stress-induced activation, microsolvation (η control), and auxiliary-mediated interfaces influence reaction kinetics, selectivity, and scalability. Emerging platforms, such as twin-screw extrusion (TSE), resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), and bead mills, extend these advantages toward scale-up and, in the case of TSE, continuous manufacturing, bridging laboratory-scale discoveries and industrial applications. Mechanochemistry functions both as a practical enabling platform and as a conceptual framework for Green Chemistry, embracing atom economy, solvent reduction, and operational safety within a unified solid-state synthetic framework.

shortlist.title: Cationic Ionomer Coatings Promote Anion Electroreduction: Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Electrolysis technologies represent a promising pathway to valorize abundant feedstocks using renewable electricity. While ionomers serve critical roles as ion conductors and catalyst binders in electrolyzers, their impact on electrochemical transformations of ionic species remains poorly understood compared to extensively studied neutral-molecule conversions like water splitting and CO2 reduction. Herein, we use the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction as a model transformation to investigate the influence of ionomer coatings in anion electroreduction reactions, which face fundamental challenges from electrostatic anion depletion near negatively polarized cathodes and premature desorption of anionic intermediates. We demonstrate that cationic ionomer coatings increase local nitrate concentration up to 10-fold compared to bulk electrolyte due to the interfacial Donnan potential. While prior studies have shown that ionomers can influence the local reaction microenvironment, this work provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first quantitative measurement of nitrate concentration within ionomer coatings as a function of charge density and its impact on catalysis. A 5-fold enhancement in ammonium partial current density was achieved with the ionomer bearing the highest charge density. Using in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), we quantified enhanced local nitrate concentration (up to 1.1 M versus 0.1 M in bulk electrolyte), conversion, and supply with increasing charge density. This study establishes guiding principles for tuning ionomer charge identity and density to control interfacial ion concentrations in electrochemical transformations of dilute charged substrates.

shortlist.title: Magnetic Resonance Silent Activatable Probe with Massive Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated Fibrogenesis
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Biomarker-specific molecular imaging is vital in precision medicine. However, a fundamental challenge of most molecular imaging methods is the difficulty of distinguishing specific molecular signal from nonspecific signal arising from the distribution of the molecular probe. This is even more pronounced in metabolically active organs such as the kidney and liver where the probe may concentrate prior to elimination. As a result, almost all molecular imaging relies on delayed imaging to achieve specificity, but this constrains clinical throughput and impedes rapid assessment of the diseased organ. Here, we report a magnetic resonance (MR) probe, Fe(II)-IAFP2, which combines 3 drivers of relaxivity enhancement to decouple disease specificity from probe distribution. Fe(II)-IAFP2 is MR-silent in its Fe(II) state, producing negligible MR signal even at high concentrations. In inflammatory, fibrogenic microenvironments common to many diseases, rapid oxidation to Fe(III) activates MR enhancement, while reversible aldehyde-mediated binding to remodeled extracellular matrix further amplifies relaxivity and promotes retention at the site of tissue injury. This dual activation–retention mechanism enables robust signal generation within minutes of administration. In mouse models of renal and liver fibrogenesis, Fe(II)-IAFP2 generated disease-associated MR contrast within minutes after intravenous administration. Together, this work demonstrates an effective strategy for rapid, activity-based molecular MR imaging through the combination of pathological activation and complementary tissue retention.

shortlist.title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets
shortlist.abstract: This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

shortlist.title: Unifying Polar and Hydrophobic Models of Ice Recognition by Antifreeze Glycoproteins
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Antifreeze glycoproteins (AFGPs) enable polar organisms to survive at subzero temperatures by inhibiting ice growth through selective association with specific crystallographic planes. However, the molecular basis of this interaction and its remarkable selectivity remain incompletely understood, and both polar and hydrophobic binding models have been proposed. Here, we combine the synthesis of AFGP variants with high-resolution NMR spectroscopy, antifreeze activity measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the molecular determinants of ice recognition. Minimally perturbative chemical modifications, including site-specific deuteration and fluorination, were used to probe the contributions of nonpolar and polar interactions while preserving the characteristic AFGP conformation. The combined structure–activity relationships and computational analyses support an integrative binding model that provides a unified and parsimonious interpretation of the experimental observations. Within this framework, our experimental evidence is consistent with the view that dispersive interactions involving peptide and carbohydrate methyl groups favor productive association with the ice surface, whereas carbohydrate hydroxyl groups, together with sugar- and backbone-associated water molecules, contribute polar interactions that promote selective and persistent binding. This model reconciles key aspects of previously proposed polar and hydrophobic descriptions and provides a molecular rationale for the characteristic plane selectivity of AFGPs and the conservation of specific sequence motifs. shortlist.title: Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity
shortlist.abstract: BACKGROUND: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for the treatment of painful knee osteoarthritis in persons with obesity. METHODS: In two phase 3 trials, adults without diabetes who had painful knee osteoarthritis and a body-mass index of at least 27 were randomly assigned to receive once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide (9 or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-4 and 4, 9, or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-1-OA) or placebo. In TRIUMPH-4, the primary end points were the change in the WOMAC pain score (range, 0 to 10, with higher scores indicating worse pain) and the percent change in body weight at week 68. In TRIUMPH-1-OA, the primary end point was the change in the WOMAC pain score at week 80. For non-pain-related end points, intercurrent events were handled with a treatment-policy strategy. For pain-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy for intercurrent events that suggested treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy elsewhere. We also report results for an intention-to-treat (ITT) estimand. RESULTS: A total of 445 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-4 and 574 in TRIUMPH-1-OA. At 68 weeks, the mean changes in the WOMAC pain score (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-4 were -3.96 (9 mg) and -3.74 (12 mg), versus -2.12 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -1.83 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -2.37 to -1.30] and -1.61 [95% CI, -2.16 to -1.07], respectively). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -1.70 (95% CI, -2.19 to -1.22) and -1.38 (95% CI, -1.91 to -0.85) (P<0.001 for all comparisons). The mean percent changes in body weight with retatrutide were -20.0% (9 mg) and -23.7% (12 mg), versus -4.6% with placebo…

shortlist.title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease
shortlist.abstract: BACKGROUND: The inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 is hypothesized to be a therapeutic target for patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Whether neutralizing interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab, a monoclonal antibody, reduces the risk of adverse cardiovascular events remains unknown. METHODS: We conducted a multinational, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation (defined by a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [CRP] level of ≥2 mg per liter). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ziltivekimab (15 mg once monthly) or placebo. The primary efficacy end point was a 3-point major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE). This composite end point included death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke. RESULTS: A total of 6376 patients were included in the full analysis population: 3184 were assigned to receive ziltivekimab and 3192 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 69.4 years, and 27.5% were women. At 24 months, the between-group difference in the median percent change in the levels of inflammatory biomarkers among patients receiving ziltivekimab as compared with those receiving placebo was -76 percentage points for free interleukin-6 and -64 percentage points for high-sensitivity CRP. During a median follow-up of 33 months, a primary end-point event occurred in 561 patients (17.6%) in the ziltivekimab group and in 565 patients (17.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.99; 95% confidence interval, 0.88 to 1.11; P = 0.84). Serious adverse events occurred in 54.6% of the patients in the ziltivekimab…

shortlist.title: Landau Damping and Plasma Echoes
shortlist.abstract: This review article provides an overview and the state of the art of the study of Landau damping and plasma echoes in the classical Vlasov–Poisson system near spatially homogeneous equilibria that describes the dynamics of a plasma confined on a torus or in the whole space. In particular, the article reproduces an analyticity framework developed for nonspecialists in [E. Grenier, T. T. Nguyen, and I. Rodnianski, SIAM J. Math. Anal., 54 (2022), pp. 940–953] that constructs plasma echo solutions consisting of infinitely many interacting elementary waves with arbitrarily high frequencies. The echo solutions allow a much larger class of data than those in analytic or Gevrey spaces studied by Mouhot and Villani, now including certain data with arbitrarily large Sobolev norms; nonetheless, these solutions do exhibit Landau damping in the large time.

shortlist.title: Abstract 13530: Factor XI/XIa Inhibitors for Secondary Prevention After Non-Cardioembolic Ischemic Stroke and High-Risk Transient Ischemic Attack: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
shortlist.abstract: Background: Factor XI/Xia inhibitors have gained attention as an innovative anticoagulant strategy which may reduce thrombosis without substantially impairing hemostasis. Their role in secondary prevention following non-cardioembolic stroke and high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA) remains uncertain. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trial (RCTs) assessing the efficacy and safety of factor XI/Xia inhibition in patient with these conditions. Research Question: Does treatment with factor XI/XIa inhibitors improve clinical outcomes while minimizing bleeding complications compared with conventional therapy in patients with non-cardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA? Methods: A thorough search was performed on PubMed, Scopus, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov and the Cochrane library from inception until May 2025 comparing Factor XI/XIa inhibitors, primarily asundexian and milvexian, with placebo or standard antithrombotic therapy in patients with non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA. Pooled Risk Ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were computed using random-effects models. Results: Five RCTs involving 18,603 participants were included. Factor XI/XIa inhibitors were associated with a significant reduction in symptomatic ischemic stroke compared with control therapy (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.86; p<0.00001; I 2 =0%). No significant differences were observed for the composite of symptomatic ischemic stroke and covert infarction (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87-1.18; p=0.89; I 2 =0%) or the composite of symptomatic ischemic stroke and TIA (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.61-1.01; p=0.06; I 2 =0%). shortlist.title: The commutativity problem for effective varieties of formal series, and applications
shortlist.abstract: A formal series in noncommuting variables Σ over the rationals is a mapping Σ * → Q from the free monoid generated by Σ to the rationals. We say that it is commutative if the output does not depend on the order of the symbols in the input. The commutativity problem for a class of series takes as input a (finite presentation of) a series from the class and amounts to establishing whether it is commutative. This is a very natural, albeit nontrivial problem, which has not been considered before from an algorithmic perspective. We show that commutativity is decidable for all classes of series that constitute a so-called effective prevariety , a notion generalising Reutenauer’s varieties of formal series. For example, the class of rational series , introduced by Schützenberger in the 1960’s, is well-known to be an effective (pre)variety, and thus commutativity is decidable for it. In order to showcase the applicability of our result, we consider classes of formal series generalising the rational ones. We consider polynomial automata , shuffle automata , and infiltration automata , and we show that each of these models recognises an effective prevariety of formal series. Consequently, their commutativity problem is decidable, which is a novel result. We find it remarkable that commutativity can be decided in a uniform way for such disparate computation models. Finally, we present applications of commutativity outside the theory of formal series. We show that we can decide solvability in sequences and in power series for restricted classes of algebraic difference and differential equations, for which such problems are undecidable in full generality. Thanks to this, we can prove that the syntaxes of multivariate polynomial recursive sequences and of constructible…

shortlist.title: Abstract 15126: Elective Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump Ranks Highest for Survival in High-Risk Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials
shortlist.abstract: Background: The optimal mechanical circulatory support strategy for patients undergoing high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains uncertain. Randomized trials evaluating elective intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), Impella, and standard care have reported conflicting results and have not been synthesized within a unified comparative framework. Research Question/Hypothesis: We evaluated the comparative efficacy and safety of elective IABP, Impella, and standard care in planned high-risk PCI. Methods: We systematically identified randomized controlled trials enrolling patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction undergoing planned high-risk PCI. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis compared elective IABP, Impella, and standard care. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included periprocedural myocardial injury, major bleeding, vascular complications, spontaneous myocardial infarction, and stroke. Results: Three randomized trials (BCIS-1, PROTECT II, and CHIP-BCIS3) comprising 1,053 patients formed a closed triangular evidence network. Model convergence was excellent (all R̂<1.01), with low estimated between-study heterogeneity (posterior median τ=0.346). For all-cause mortality, elective IABP demonstrated the most favorable treatment profile. Compared with standard care, IABP was associated with a 40% reduction in mortality odds (OR 0.60, 95% CrI 0.24-1.31) and an 89.7% posterior probability of benefit. This signal remained consistent across prespecified sensitivity analyses, including long-term follow-up data (OR 0.64, 95% CrI 0.29-1.30; probability of benefit 91.4%). shortlist.title: Abstract 15652: Left Bundle Branch Pacing versus Biventricular Pacing for Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy in Heart Failure with Left Bundle Branch Block: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
shortlist.abstract: Background: Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) via biventricular pacing (BiVP) is established as a guideline-directed intervention for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and left bundle branch block (LBBB). Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) has emerged as a physiological alternative that directly recruits the native His-Purkinje conduction system, potentially delivering superior electrical and mechanical resynchronization. Despite growing observational evidence, randomized trial data comparing LBBP and BiVP remain limited. This meta-analysis synthesizes all available randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. We searched PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to June 2026. Two independent reviewers screened studies and extracted data. We included prospective RCTs comparing dedicated LBBP with BiVP in adults with HFrEF and LBBB. The primary outcome was the change in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) from baseline. Secondary outcomes included super-response rate, heart failure hospitalization (HFH), all-cause mortality, paced QRS duration, and safety. We used random-effects to do the analysis and assessed heterogeneity with the I 2 statistic. Results: Two RCTs met full eligibility criteria, enrolling a total of 240 patients. Both trials enrolled patients with nonischemic cardiomyopathy predominating and LBBB. Pooled analysis showed that LBBP was associated with significantly greater LVEF improvement compared with BiVP (mean difference: +6.1%; 95% CI: 1.6%-10.6%; P=0.007; I 2 =0%). shortlist.title: Harnessing Contact Electrification and Static Charge for Chemical Reactions: Fundamentals and Applications of Contact Electrocatalysis
shortlist.abstract: The chemical industry is the largest industrial energy consumer and the third-largest emitter of CO2 globally. Despite efforts to enhance energy efficiency, many chemical reactions still require significant external energy due to fundamental thermodynamic barriers. Thus, transitioning to a sustainable chemical industry requires new renewable energy or catalytic technologies that reduce energy demand. In catalytic systems, flowing liquids, moving parts, and gas separation mean local static charge is often generated on the nanoscale. This review explores the static charge formation at solid–solid, solid–liquid, and solid–gas interfaces, such as those that occur in catalytic reactions, and then extends this discussion to a deeper focus on how these generated static charges can be used for catalysis, including electrostatic catalysis, static charge electrochemistry, and contact electrocatalysis (CEC). CEC, where motion-induced charge separation leads to local static charge formation, is then specifically examined, exploring why and how it has emerged as an exciting tool to enable these green chemical transformations. The focus is to highlight the most recent developments in CEC, with mechanistic interpretation, factors that affect CEC performance, and emerging applications, and to provide outlook and guidance for the field─specifically highlighting the need to build structure–property relationships for CEC performance and static charge formation for target chemical reactions.

shortlist.title: Abstract 10888: Clinical Outcomes of Novel Aldosterone Synthase Inhibitors (Lorundrostat and Baxdrostat) in Low and High Dose in Uncontrolled Hypertension: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of RCTs
shortlist.abstract: Background: Despite the availability of antihypertensive therapies, uncontrolled and resistant hypertension remains common, possibly driven by inappropriate aldosterone activity. Novel aldosterone synthase inhibitors (ASIs) such as Lorundrostat and Baxdrostat selectively inhibit CYP11B2, offering to reduce aldosterone production without effects of MRAs (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists). This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of ASIs in patients with uncontrolled hypertension. Methods: We systematically searched Pubmed, Google scholar Cochrane library and clinicaltrials.gov from inception to February 2026 for RCTs evaluating Lorundrostat or Baxdrostat versus placebo in adults with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension. The primary outcome was the change in SBP (systolic blood pressure) from baseline to study endpoint. Secondary outcomes included mean change in diastolic blood pressure (DBP) and safety events such as adverse effects and discontinuations. Random effect model was employed and RevMan software version 5.4 was used. Risk of Bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB-2 tool. Results: Five RCTS with 2439 patients were included. Compared to placebo high dose ASIs (Lorundrostat 100mg or Baxdrostat 1-2mg) significantly reduced SBP at 6-8 weeks by -7.93mm Hg, 95% CI: -930 to -6.56; I2= 0%, Figure 1 and at 10-12 weeks by -9.49 mm Hg, 95% CI -11.96 to -7.03; I2= 0%) Low dose ASIs (Lorundrostat 50mg or Baxdrostat 0.5 mg) also reduced SBP at 10-12 weeks by -7.23 mmHg, 95% CI: -9.98 to -4.48; I2=0%) Figure 2. The overall pooled SBP reduction was -8.57mm Hg, 95% CI -9.74, -7.21). DBP reduction was -4.36mm Hg. shortlist.title: Beyond Lithiophilicity: Multistage Rate Matching in Lithium‐Metal Electrodeposition
shortlist.abstract: Lithium (Li)‐metal deposition is commonly interpreted using static descriptors, including lithiophilicity, nucleation overpotential, ionic conductivity, or solid‐electrolyte interphase composition. Although these parameters provide valuable insights, none alone determines how an initially nucleated Li deposit evolves under sustained current. Here, we conceptualize Li electrodeposition as a dynamically coupled sequence involving Li + transport, interfacial entry, charge transfer, Li 0 surface redistribution, nucleation, and growth; desolvation is an interfacial‐entry process in liquid electrolytes. Li 0 surface redistribution denotes the lateral motion of newly reduced Li species before incorporation into a growing deposit, with surface diffusion as one possible mechanism. Uniform deposition requires multidimensional kinetic compatibility across these stages, rather than maximization of any individual step. In particular, Li 0 surface redistribution can bridge initial nucleation and subsequent lateral growth, while the decay of morphological perturbations provides a conceptual criterion for deposition stability. From this perspective, solvent chemistry, anions, additives, concentrated electrolytes, polymers, and solid electrolytes can be understood as upstream regulators that reshape the coupled rate chain. This framework shifts lithium‐metal design from optimizing isolated material properties toward engineering a dynamically self‐leveling deposition field through multistage rate matching.

shortlist.title: Transition-Metal-Catalyzed Multicomponent Cycloadditions
shortlist.abstract: Transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions provide a powerful strategy for constructing complex cyclic frameworks from simple unsaturated building blocks with high atom and step efficiencies. This Review highlights the progress made in transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions based on the size of the cyclic products formed. First, reactions that construct five-membered rings, including [2 + 2 + 1], [3 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 1 + 1] cycloadditions, are discussed with an emphasis on key reactive intermediates, such as carbon monoxide, vinylidenes, carbenoids, and nitrenes. Next, six-membered-ring-forming processes, particularly [2 + 2 + 2], [3 + 2 + 1], [4 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions, are described, highlighting combinations of alkynes, alkenes, and heteroatom-containing components. The Review then covers strategies for constructing seven-membered rings via [3 + 2 + 2] and [4 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions. Finally, emerging methods that enable the formation of eight- and nine-membered rings through higher-order multicomponent cycloadditions are described. This Review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the conceptual framework, mechanistic principles, and synthetic possibilities of transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions by organizing them according to ring size and cycloaddition components.

shortlist.title: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
shortlist.abstract: Genetic effects on gene expression often vary across cell types, motivating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Existing approaches generally aggregate expression across cells, use Gaussian models poorly suited to read counts or do not scale. Here we show that SAIGE-QTL, a Poisson mixed model that directly models single-cell read counts, enables calibrated and computationally scalable eQTL mapping while accounting for donor-level and cell-level covariates and unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three single-cell datasets, SAIGE-QTL improved statistical efficiency and discovery of genes with significant eQTLs (eGenes) relative to pseudobulk methods and produced results consistent with existing single-cell models at substantially lower computational cost. In 1.2 million immune cells, SAIGE-QTL identified 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. SAIGE-QTL further enabled genome-wide trans-eQTL mapping and rare variant set-based testing, identifying rare variant associations independent of common eQTL signals. SAIGE-QTL therefore expands single-cell eQTL discovery across common, rare and trans-acting genetic variation.

shortlist.title: Participatory Budgeting in Public Health: Promise, Evidence, Challenges, and Opportunities
shortlist.abstract: Participatory budgeting (PB) is a deliberative decision-making process that invites community participation to direct spending for a defined portion of public budgets. Originating in Brazil in the 1980s, PB has since diffused across the globe, including several hundred cases in the United States and Canada alone. PB programs vary but are generally characterized by five core principles: voice, vote, social inclusion, social justice, and oversight. Research on PB shows promising though moderate associations with improved population health outcomes, including infant mortality reductions and health and sanitation spending increases. Despite PB's conceptual alignment with many public health values, adoption of PB by US public health agencies remains limited, constrained by categorical funding requirements, small discretionary budgets, and a polarized sociopolitical environment. This article reviews PB's conceptual foundations, evidence base, and real-world applications before examining structural and political challenges and opportunities for PB as a means to improve the public's health.

shortlist.title: Proximal redox coupling enables oxidation damping for stable water electrolysis
shortlist.abstract: The design of atomically precise catalysts requires strategies that regulate their electronic and structural dynamics under operating conditions. While conventional doping can effectively tune bulk materials, it translates poorly to single-atom catalysts (SACs), in which isolated atoms lack extended coordination and are prone to oxidative instability. Here we design atomically dispersed Ru−O−Cr motifs that enable oxidation damping during acidic oxygen evolution. In situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy shows attenuated Ru oxidation synchronized with anticorrelated and partially reversible Cr redox evolution, consistent with proximity-dependent redox coupling. This buffered redox response is accompanied by bounded and partially reversible changes in the local metal−oxygen coordination environment. These coupled dynamics support proximity-coupled Ru−O−Cr redox units, enabling a 55.7-fold increased resistance against oxidation-induced Ru dissolution compared with conventional SACs. In proton exchange membrane water electrolysis, catalysts incorporating proximal Ru−O−Cr configurations exhibit degradation rates that are 6.8-fold and 14.4-fold lower than those of Ru SACs and commercial RuO2, respectively, at 1 A cm−2. These results suggest proximal oxidation damping as a potential design principle for stabilizing atomically precise electrocatalysts. Single-atom catalysts can mitigate reliance on scarce noble metals, but isolated sites can be fragile. Here a catalyst with proximal Ru−O−Cr motifs is fabricated that demonstrates proximal oxidation damping where the Cr neighbour buffers Ru overoxidation, improving stability for acidic oxygen evolution.

shortlist.title: Optimal learning of quantum channels in diamond distance
shortlist.abstract: The evolution of quantum states can be described by quantum channels. The task of estimating an unknown quantum channel, known as process tomography, is a central problem in quantum information theory. A long-standing open question is how many uses of an unknown channel are required to learn it to a precision quantified by the standard metric for distinguishing quantum processes, known as the diamond distance. Here we address this by establishing the query complexity of channel tomography with optimal dependence on the dimensions of the input and output spaces and the channel’s Kraus rank at any fixed constant accuracy in diamond distance. We design an algorithm that establishes an upper bound and prove a matching lower bound for learning a channel to the given accuracy. Our algorithm follows the strategy of performing optimal tomography on the Choi-state representation of the process, and we show that channel tomography can be reduced to the well-studied problem of pure-state tomography. As channels subsume states, unitaries and measurements as special cases, our protocol provides a unified framework for tomography of these tasks.

fig.label: Figure 1
fig.caption: Protocol for learning quantum channels. Parallel invocations of the unknown channel Λ , applied to halves of maximally entangled states |Ω⟩ , prepare copies of its normalised Choi state Φ_c=J(Λ) . A purification channel then maps these Choi-state copies to copies of a random purification |Φ_c⟩ , which are learned using a sample-optimal pure-state tomography scheme. Finally, a classical post-processing step, formulated as a semidefinite program projecting onto the set of CPTP maps, returns a channel estimate Λ̂ satisfying ‖Λ̂-Λ‖_◇≤ε with high probability.

shortlist.title: Older yet faster: Representational development explains accelerated semantic processing in older adults.
shortlist.abstract: Slower responses in older age are often taken as evidence for cognitive decline, yet they may also stem from representational changes shaped by lifelong learning. Building on the information-accumulation perspective on aging, we argue that behavioral change across the lifespan can arise from representational systems continuously updated through learning from the environment. This view predicts that aging may bring both benefits and costs: Performance improves when task demands are congruent with accumulated knowledge but declines when they conflict. We provide convergent evidence for this account across three studies, each comprising the following components. First, in tasks requiring participants to access word meanings (i.e., when task demands were congruent with representation), we found that older adults (70-80 years old) exhibited faster semantic processing speed than younger adults (18-25 years old), a finding that cannot be explained by decline-based accounts. Second, we traced this processing advantage to systematic changes in older adults' conceptual representations inferred from semantic rating tasks. Third, using learning simulation models, we demonstrated how such representational changes could emerge naturally from cumulative language experience. Replications across different samples, task requirements, and word stimuli strengthen the robustness of these findings. Finally, we identified a boundary condition: When learned representations contain information incongruent with task demands, older adults' greater learning experience not only attenuates their representational changes but also reduces processing-speed advantage. Altogether, our research challenges the explanatory framework of cognitive aging that emphasizes decline and compensation, advancing a…

shortlist.title: Self-esteem and social relationships: A meta-analytic review of longitudinal studies with continuous time modeling.
shortlist.abstract: This preregistered systematic review investigated reciprocal effects between people's self-esteem and the quality of their social relationships by meta-analyzing the available longitudinal data. Analyses were based on 82 samples, including 86,850 participants. Mean age of samples ranged from 8 to 63 years. We used continuous time modeling to account for between-study differences in the time intervals between assessments, which ranged from 1 week to 6 years. Moreover, we controlled for stable between-person variance in the constructs via latent trait variables. The results showed positive cross-lagged effects between self-esteem and relationship quality. The effects peaked at an interval of approximately 3 months, with medium to large effect sizes of β = .13 for the effect of self-esteem on relationship quality and β = .09 for the effect of relationship quality on self-esteem. The effects had largely faded after 1 year. We tested for moderator effects of type of relationship partner, age, proportion of female participants, cultural context, and type of relationship measure. Cross-lagged effects were largest for general social relationships, followed by relationships with parents, but were smaller and close to zero for peer and romantic relationships. Age, proportion of female participants, and cultural context showed significant effects, but the magnitude of these moderator effects was small. The effects also differed by type of relationship measure, with self-reports showing larger effects than other measures. In sum, the findings support theories that emphasize the importance of social relationships for self-esteem and theories suggesting that people's self-esteem shapes the quality of their relationships. shortlist.title: An (in)complete NIRSpec census of Balmer absorption in Type 1 AGN – radiation-driven outflows in little red dots, quasars and variable stars
shortlist.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
shortlist.abstract: A notable achievement of the first generation of JWST surveys was the discovery of an abundance of faint high-redshift (z > 4) broad-line active galactic nuclei (AGN) in the Lbol < 1045 erg s−1 regime, previously only accessible at z < 1. The high prevalence of absorption features in their broad hydrogen lines is one of the peculiarities of a significant fraction of this new population. In this paper, we conduct a broad census of Balmer absorption in a sample of 47 Type-1 AGN spanning 2 < z < 7. Accounting for incompleteness of JWST spectroscopic data, we estimate that 44₋₆⁺²¹ % of Little Red Dots (LRDs) have absorption in Hα while the incidence rate is <25 % (at 2σ) in Little Blue Dots (LBDs). Additionally, R1000 JWST/NIRSpec data is strongly resolution limited, implying an inability to disentangle Doppler broadening in the absorption from optical depth effects. This is alleviated with R2700 observations, although some degeneracies remain. We find a significant correlation between the velocity of the Balmer absorption and the [OIII]5007 narrow line luminosity, suggesting a common driving mechanism. We do not find any other significant correlations (and do not confirm previously claimed correlations) between Balmer absorption and other spectral properties of LRDs (except for the expected correlation between Hα and Hβ absorption velocities). Comparing LRDs, quasars and stellar Hα absorbers, we establish that absorption in both LRDs and broad absorption line quasars is consistent with radiatively driven outflows, echoing the physics of variable stars yet occurring at vastly different scales.

shortlist.title: The Huang–Yang conjecture for the low-density Fermi gas
shortlist.abstract: Our work establishes a three-term asymptotic expansion of the ground state energy of a dilute gas of spin 1/2 1 / 2 fermions with repulsive short-range interactions, validating a formula predicted by Huang and Yang in 1957. The formula is universal in the sense that it holds for a large class of interaction potentials and depends on those only via their scattering length. We have recently proved an upper bound on the ground state energy of the desired form, and the present work completes the program by proving the matching lower bound.

shortlist.title: Optimization Problems with Nonconvexities Involving the Euclidean Norm: Challenges, Progress, and Opportunities
shortlist.abstract: The field of global optimization has advanced significantly over the past three decades, yet the solution to global optimality of even small instances of many optimization problems with nonconvexities involving the Euclidean norm remains beyond the reach of modern global optimization methods. These problems include numerous well-known and high-impact open research questions from a diverse collection of both fundamental and applied fields of science and engineering. In this review, we survey applications in which these problems arise, describe sources of computational intractability, summarize existing solution methods, and identify promising research directions for future work. We also introduce EuclidLib, a library of instances of optimization problems of this type, to aid in performance benchmarking and algorithm development. The solution to global optimality of all problems in EuclidLib would represent a significant achievement for the field of global optimization and an important contribution to mathematics, science, and engineering.

shortlist.title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
shortlist.abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01302 .

shortlist.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
shortlist.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .

shortlist.title: Tackling the Commercial Determinants of Obesity: A Review of Key Policies and Strategies
shortlist.abstract: A growing body of evidence demonstrates that commercial entities play an important role in shaping the prevalence, incidence, and distribution of obesity. This narrative review examines policy solutions to address the commercial determinants of obesity. We describe how five business sectors (food, beverages, and agriculture; media and entertainment; sports and recreation; transportation; and medical care and pharmaceuticals) shape obesity prevalence through three key behavioral pathways: diet, physical activity, and use of medical care. We then examine four categories of tools available to national and subnational governments to address the commercial determinants: legal and regulatory measures, fiscal policies, market governance mechanisms, and litigation. Finally, we discuss three strategies that can support the successful implementation of these measures: building cross-sectoral support, limiting undue influence in policymaking processes, and designing policies informed by precedent and designed to withstand challenges. We conclude by highlighting key insights for policymakers seeking to make measurable progress in preventing and reducing obesity.

shortlist.title: Private debt versus bank debt in corporate borrowing
shortlist.abstract: Using administrative bank loan-level data matched to private debt deals, we study the interaction between private and bank debt for a large segment of dual borrowers. These firms use private debt for investment and bank credit lines for liquidity insurance. Private debt carries higher spreads and commonly features flexible, equity-like terms that are associated with greater reliance on bank credit lines. Relative to bank-only borrowers, dual borrowers obtain more and larger credit lines and draw them more intensively following liquidity shocks. Our findings suggest that private debt substitutes for bank term loans but complements banks’ provision of credit lines.

shortlist.title: Labor Unions and Better Health
shortlist.abstract: Social-class inequities in health arise from power imbalances in our political-economic system. However, through labor-union organizing, workers can build power to improve their life chances and health. In our review, we describe the rich historical, theoretical, and mechanistic evidence linking unions and health and critically evaluate the state of quantitative research on the topic. Most individual-level and ecological studies have estimated small beneficial or null union-health associations. However, as we describe, the studies are limited in number, particularly outside the Global North, and face many technical and conceptual challenges, including feedback loops between unions and societies' political-economic contexts. We conclude with recommendations for enhancing the rigor and utility of union-health research, including by richly contextualizing studies' findings and by answering questions raised by workers themselves. As social and economic inequities intensify and workers face heightening attacks on their well-being, unions remain crucial organizations for advancing health justice.
