shortlist.title: Shadow banks on the rise: Evidence across market segments
shortlist.abstract: This paper examines the comparative advantages of shadow banks across market segments. Combining credit bureau data on retail loans in India with weather shocks as a proxy for credit demand, we show that Fintechs respond more in uncollateralized markets. In contrast, non-Fintech shadow banks exhibit stronger responsiveness in collateralized markets. Exploiting geographic heterogeneity in the adoption of digital payments, we identify technology as the key advantage for Fintechs. Leveraging four natural experiments, we document the significance of lower regulation for non-Fintech shadow banks. Our results suggest that the comparative advantage of shadow banks differs across market segments.

shortlist.title: Atomically resolved superconducting gap in (La,Pr) 3 Ni 2 O 7 films
shortlist.abstract: Ruddlesden-Popper bilayer nickelates provide an emerging platform for studying high-temperature superconductivity, yet the superconducting pairing symmetry remains under debate. Here, we use atomic-resolution scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy to investigate superconducting 1.5-unit-cell (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 films grown on SrLaAlO4. A cryogenic ultrahigh-vacuum (UHV) sample transfer preserves an ordered sqrt(2) * sqrt(2) surface and yields reproducible U-shaped spectra with two gap scales of ~14 and ~20 meV and extended flat zero-conductance bottoms. By contrast, samples exposed for a longer time in UHV without cooling during transfer show V-shaped spectra despite retaining the surface reconstruction and a transport superconducting transition onset above 40 K. Wide-energy-range spectra indicate that oxygen loss can mix density-wave-related spectral weight. Our measurements provide an atomic-scale observation of the intrinsic nodeless superconducting gap in bilayer nickelate ultrathin films.

shortlist.title: Benefiting from Culture Wars: Resource Mobilization in Polarized Issue Domains
shortlist.abstract: Organizations engaging with contested social issues may struggle to mobilize resources due to disapproval from hostile audiences. Yet, some may benefit from increased support from sympathetic audiences, leaving unclear when such support will outweigh opposition. We propose that variation in audience reactions depends partly on how contestation is structured. We theorize that ideological polarization—the extent to which opposing stances on an issue sort along ideological lines—may enhance resource mobilization in contested issue domains. As polarization increases, contested issues pit opposing identities against each other and heighten threats to sympathetic audiences’ worldviews. New ventures in more polarized domains may attract greater support as sympathetic audiences respond by investing in aligned ventures, a mechanism we term “compensatory investment.” This relationship strengthens under conditions that heighten identity threat: when issues are highly salient, making them central political battlegrounds, and when audiences on both sides rely on core moral foundations to evaluate the issue, so that disagreements are experienced as moral violations. Analyses of U.S.-based Kickstarter campaigns (2009–2020) support our predictions and provide evidence consistent with compensatory investment. Our study highlights polarization as a key source of issue heterogeneity, introduces the mechanism of compensatory investment, and specifies when polarization enhances resource mobilization.

shortlist.title: Controlling Rydberg atom-polariton interactions: from exceptional points to fast readout
shortlist.abstract: Rydberg atoms represent a platform underpinning many recent developments in quantum computation, simulation, sensing, and metrology. They further facilitate optical nonlinearity at the single-photon level when coupled to photons propagating in atomic clouds, which form collective atomic excitations called Rydberg polaritons, strongly interacting with each other. Here, we experimentally explore interactions between a Rydberg polariton in an atomic ensemble and a single, adjacent, Rydberg atom. We discover three different regimes of quantum dynamics corresponding to polariton blockade, coherent exchange, and probabilistic hopping, which are defined by their distinct transmission characteristics, with a transition through an exceptional point occurring between blockade and coherent exchange. We investigate the applications of such interactions for fast, non-destructive detection of Rydberg atoms and present proof-of-principle demonstrations for their potential application in nonlinear photonic networks.

shortlist.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
shortlist.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. shortlist.title: Dynamics of O(2) excitations in a non-reciprocal medium
shortlist.abstract: We investigate emergent dynamics due to non-reciprocity in the O(2) model. The lattice XY model, where non-reciprocity stems from vision cone like couplings, can be described by a continuum description in which non-reciprocity translates into a new term depending on the rotational of the orientation field. We argue that non-reciprocity is akin to activity and we highlight the connection between our hydrodynamic equation and the constant density Toner-Tu framework. The active force advects and reshapes patterns, a generic feature found in many non-reciprocal systems. We show how 1d excitations in the non-reciprocal O(2) model can be described by a generalized Burgers equation, derived from our continuum model. We then extend the results to 2d perturbations. As such, we establish the first principles of excitation trajectory control in a non-reciprocal O(2) medium. Concretely, we explain how tuning the degree of non-reciprocity and the orientation of the background medium impacts the time evolution of excitations. We also showcase how initially different excitations lead to very different dynamical behavior. Non-reciprocity also affects the stability of defect-free excitations with non-zero winding numbers and, unlike in its equilibrium O(2) counterpart, enables the system, above a certain threshold, to relax to its ground state.

shortlist.title: How to raise a supermassive black hole: interpreting early JWST AGN with the AESOPICA simulations
shortlist.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
shortlist.abstract: The active galactic nuclei (AGN) uncovered by JWST in the early Universe are highly abundant and seemingly overmassive with respect to local scaling relations, challenging standard models of black hole formation and growth. Yet it remains unclear whether they trace an efficient early growth channel, represent the observable tail of a broader population, or reflect systematic uncertainties in mass estimates. We introduce the aesopica project, a suite of twelve mid-volume (L = 60 cMpc) cosmological simulations based on the fable galaxy formation model, varying the black hole seed mass across the theoretical formation channels (Mseed = 102–105 M⊙), the accretion efficiency, including super-Eddington bursts, and the supernova feedback strength. We forward-model observational selection with balmersopica, a mock JWST broad-line survey pipeline that assesses the detectability of each simulated AGN for a given grating and exposure time. We find that the bulk of the JWST AGN population can be assembled from any seed mass provided the accretion efficiency is high, although light seeds require the most favourable accretion conditions explored. Applying broad-line selection naturally recovers the apparently overmassive population, with the detected AGN lying furthest above the intrinsic MBH–Mstellar relation for inefficient accretion models. The selected AGN lie on the local, weakly evolving MBH–σstellar relation, supporting a scenario where black holes assemble before the stellar component is fully established. Since efficient accretion rapidly erases the imprint of the initial seed mass, the low-mass end of the black hole mass function and host gas-phase metallicities offer the most promising discriminants between seeding channels.

shortlist.title: A two-phase model of galaxy formation: IV. Seeding and growing supermassive black holes in dark matter halos
shortlist.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
shortlist.abstract: We present a theoretical framework for seeding and growing supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in dark matter halos along their assembly histories. Seeds are bred out of Pop-III stars formed during the first collapse of pristine gas in mini-halos that have reached the H2-cooling limit, modulated by UV radiation from star formation and dynamical heating from fast halo assembly. Such breeding persists until the enrichment of the intergalactic medium (IGM) enables Pop-II stars to form. Post-seeding growth of black holes (BHs) is driven by distinct channels, starting with episodic super-Eddington accretion associated with nuclear bursts induced by global disturbances of galaxies, followed by sustained sub-Eddington accretion via capturing sub-clouds formed in self-gravitating gas clouds (SGCs) in halos of fast assembly, and ending with merger-dominated, quiescent growth. We implement the model in subhalo merger trees to build a coherent framework to follow SMBH-galaxy-halo co-evolution across the whole history and structural hierarchy. BH seeds are bred with a broad mass spectrum of M_(BH)= 10–105 M⊙ at z ≈ 20–30 in mini-halos with masses of 105–108 M⊙. Nuclear bursts provide the key condition for seeds to grow into SMBHs. The M_(BH)-M* relation is a multi-piece, redshift-dependent function shaped by the interplay among different growth channels. Our model predictions are broadly consistent with existing observations; in particular, a population of BHs reminiscent of ‘little red dots’ (LRDs) discovered by JWST naturally results from the seeding and growing processes. Potential future tests of the model are discussed.

shortlist.title: Clumps in a Cocoon: Geometry and Mixing Set the Universal X-ray to Hα Surface Brightness Ratio
shortlist.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
shortlist.abstract: Recent observations reveal a nearly universal X-ray to Hα surface-brightness ratio, SBX/SBHα ~ 3, in galactic winds, ram-pressure-stripped tails, and cluster filaments. This is surprising, given the very different temperatures traced by the X-ray and Hα emission. Plane-parallel mixing-layer models do not recover this ratio. We run 3D wind-tunnel simulations in the high density-contrast (χ ~ 103) regime, where the cold phase shatters into small Hα-emitting clumps embedded in a volume-filling X-ray cocoon. After smoothing on the tail-width scale, the simulated ratio converges to the observed value. The hot-gas entrainment rate sets the bolometric luminosity, L_(bol) ∝ Mᵢₙ. Hα carries a nearly fixed fraction of this luminosity, set mainly by atomic emissivity near 104 K. The X-ray-emitting mass is the same entrainment rate multiplied by the residence time in the X-ray-emitting temperature band, and its luminosity is the corresponding thermal energy divided by the cooling time. Hence L_X∝ Mᵢₙ ∝ L_(bol), with the X-ray fraction set by the residence-to-cooling-time ratio. An age diagnostic constrains the residence time to be far shorter than the cooling time, making the X-ray and Hα fractions comparable. Their common scaling with Lbol explains the correlation, while the comparable bolometric fractions explain why the observed ratio is order unity.

The H α -emitting gas consists of numerous small clumps, while the X-ray-emitting gas is volume-filling and forms an elongated, cocoon-like structure that envelopes the H α -emitting clumps. We refer to this morphology as "clumps in a cocoon" throughout this letter.

shortlist.title: Saturation genome editing of BRCA1 across cell types improves interpretation of variant pathogenicity
shortlist.abstract: Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants.

fundamentals.title: Operator structure of power corrections and anomalous scaling in energy correlators
fundamentals.abstract: Energy correlators offer a clean probe of quantum chromodynamics, serving as an ideal laboratory to rigorously investigate non-perturbative power corrections. The recent discovery that linear corrections exhibit a universal anomalous scaling points to a deep, underlying theoretical structure. We uncover the quantum field-theoretic origin of this phenomenon in the energy-energy correlator using light-ray operators. Through an explicit loop calculation, we derive the one-loop anomalous dimension, revealing that the dijet operator must be combined with a specific triple-jet component. This provides a first-principles framework that connects operator theory with high-precision collider phenomenology.
fundamentals.topic: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

fundamentals.title: Unified theory of quartz tuning fork resonators
fundamentals.abstract: Quartz tuning forks, functioning as electrically driven piezoelectric resonators, have long served as exceptionally stable and widely adopted timing references in diverse domains of research and industry. Yet, experimentally measured electrical resonance spectra often exhibit resonance evolutions that remain unexplained within existing theoretical descriptions. Here we develop a unified continuum electromechanical modal framework that integrates piezoelectric electrodynamics, variational structural dynamics, and symmetry-selected electromechanical observability. Our theory shows quantitative agreement with experimental results, demonstrating that electrical observability emerges not from the underlying mechanical eigenmodes alone. The resulting framework unifies conventional coupled-oscillator, equivalent-circuit, and continuum descriptions within a single first-principles theory and provides a rigorous basis for precision electromechanical characterization.

fundamentals.title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
fundamentals.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
fundamentals.abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub-grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert-vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub-grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity…

fundamentals.title: Microscopic theory of phonon polaritons and long-wavelength dielectric response
fundamentals.abstract: We present a first-principles approach for calculating phonon-polariton dispersion relations. In this approach, phonon-photon interaction is described by quantization of a Hamiltonian that describes harmonic lattice vibrations coupled with the electromagnetic field inside the material. All Hamiltonian parameters are obtained from first-principles calculations, with diagonalization leading to non-interacting polariton quasiparticles. This method naturally includes retardation effects and resolves non-analytical behavior and ambiguities in phonon frequencies at the Brillouin zone center, especially in non-cubic and optically anisotropic materials. Furthermore, by incorporating higher-order terms in the Hamiltonian, we also account for quasiparticle interactions and spectral broadening. Specifically, we show how anharmonic effects in phonon polaritons lead to a dielectric response that challenges traditional models. The accuracy and consequences of the approach are demonstrated on GaP and GaN as harmonic test systems and PbTe and β-Ga₂O₃ as anharmonic test systems.

fundamentals.title: Optimal learning of quantum channels in diamond distance
fundamentals.abstract: The evolution of quantum states can be described by quantum channels. The task of estimating an unknown quantum channel, known as process tomography, is a central problem in quantum information theory. A long-standing open question is how many uses of an unknown channel are required to learn it to a precision quantified by the standard metric for distinguishing quantum processes, known as the diamond distance. Here we address this by establishing the query complexity of channel tomography with optimal dependence on the dimensions of the input and output spaces and the channel’s Kraus rank at any fixed constant accuracy in diamond distance. We design an algorithm that establishes an upper bound and prove a matching lower bound for learning a channel to the given accuracy. Our algorithm follows the strategy of performing optimal tomography on the Choi-state representation of the process, and we show that channel tomography can be reduced to the well-studied problem of pure-state tomography. As channels subsume states, unitaries and measurements as special cases, our protocol provides a unified framework for tomography of these tasks.

fig.label: Figure 1
fig.caption: Protocol for learning quantum channels. Parallel invocations of the unknown channel Λ , applied to halves of maximally entangled states |Ω⟩ , prepare copies of its normalised Choi state Φ_c=J(Λ) . A purification channel then maps these Choi-state copies to copies of a random purification |Φ_c⟩ , which are learned using a sample-optimal pure-state tomography scheme. Finally, a classical post-processing step, formulated as a semidefinite program projecting onto the set of CPTP maps, returns a channel estimate Λ̂ satisfying ‖Λ̂-Λ‖_◇≤ε with high probability.

fundamentals.title: Sound propagation in striped supersolid gases at zero temperature
fundamentals.abstract: The role of dimensionality in the identification of sound modes in many-body systems characterized by the spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry is a topic of high interdisciplinary interest in both classical and quantum systems. The emergence of stripes in superfluids is a particularly interesting example where the dimensionality of the system differs from the one of the crystal phase. Here we present a unified hydrodynamic approach for the sound propagation in the stripe phase realized in ultracold dipolar and spin-orbit-coupled Bose gases at zero temperature. Despite the deep difference of the two platforms at a microscopic level, a similar hydrodynamic description can be formulated at a macroscopic level. The main difference between the two platforms is the lack of Galilean invariance in the spin-orbit case, resulting in a different identification of the normal (non-superfluid) component of the density. In both cases the spectrum comprises two sounds, reflecting the spontaneous breaking of the U(1) and translational symmetries. Both sounds exhibit an anisotropic behavior. A comparison with the first and second sounds of the smectic-A liquid crystal is also presented.

fundamentals.title: The Huang–Yang conjecture for the low-density Fermi gas
fundamentals.abstract: Our work establishes a three-term asymptotic expansion of the ground state energy of a dilute gas of spin 1/2 1 / 2 fermions with repulsive short-range interactions, validating a formula predicted by Huang and Yang in 1957. The formula is universal in the sense that it holds for a large class of interaction potentials and depends on those only via their scattering length. We have recently proved an upper bound on the ground state energy of the desired form, and the present work completes the program by proving the matching lower bound.

fundamentals.title: Similarity Solutions of Shock Formation for First-Order Strictly Hyperbolic Systems
fundamentals.abstract: Shocks due to hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) appear throughout mathematics and science. The canonical example is shock formation in the inviscid Burgers equation [Formula: see text]. Previous studies have shown that when shocks form for the inviscid Burgers equation, for positions and times close to the shock singularity, the dynamics are locally self-similar and universal, i.e., dynamics are equivalent regardless of the initial conditions. In this paper, we show that, in fact, shock formation is self-similar and universal for general first-order strictly hyperbolic PDEs in one spatial dimension, and the self-similarity is like that of the inviscid Burgers equation. An analytical formula is derived for the self-similar universal solution. Reproducibility of computational results. This paper has been awarded the “SIAM Reproducibility Badge: Code and data available” as a recognition that the authors have followed reproducibility principles valued by SIREV and the scientific computing community. Code and data that allow readers to reproduce the results in this paper are available at https://doi.org/10.34770/6vgh-br25 and in the supplementary materials ( M180373_SM.zip [25.7MB]). fundamentals.title: Named Reactions under Mechanochemical Conditions: A Critical Survey
fundamentals.abstract: Mechanochemistry has progressed from a niche interest to a core method for solvent-free synthesis, providing sustainable and mechanistically unique alternatives to traditional solution-based chemistry. When controlled impact, shear, or vibrational energy is applied under solvent-free or solvent-lean conditions, reactions are promoted within dynamically renewed interfacial regions, revealing new patterns of selectivity, energy efficiency, and process design. This review surveys the historical development, fundamental principles, and analytical frameworks of mechanochemistry, together with an extensive compilation of named organic reactions conducted under mechanochemical conditions. By comparing mechanochemical reactions with their solution-phase counterparts, this review clarifies how stress-induced activation, microsolvation (η control), and auxiliary-mediated interfaces influence reaction kinetics, selectivity, and scalability. Emerging platforms, such as twin-screw extrusion (TSE), resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), and bead mills, extend these advantages toward scale-up and, in the case of TSE, continuous manufacturing, bridging laboratory-scale discoveries and industrial applications. Mechanochemistry functions both as a practical enabling platform and as a conceptual framework for Green Chemistry, embracing atom economy, solvent reduction, and operational safety within a unified solid-state synthetic framework.

fundamentals.title: Differentiable Programming for Differential Equations: A Review
fundamentals.abstract: The differentiable programming paradigm is a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. It refers to numerical methods for computing the gradient of a numerical model’s output. Many scientific models are based on differential equations, in which differentiable programming plays a crucial role in calculating model sensitivities, inverting model parameters, and training hybrid models that combine differential equations with data-driven approaches. Furthermore, recognizing the strong synergies between inverse methods and machine learning offers the opportunity to establish a coherent framework applicable to both fields. Differentiating functions based on the numerical solution of differential equations is nontrivial. Numerous methods based on a wide variety of paradigms have been proposed in the literature, each with pros and cons specific to the type of problem investigated. Here, we provide a comprehensive review of existing techniques to compute derivatives of numerical solutions of differential equations. We first discuss the importance of gradients of solutions of differential equations in a variety of scientific domains. Second, we lay out and compare the mathematical foundations of the various approaches. Third, we cover computational considerations and explore the solutions available in modern scientific software. Last but not least, we provide best practices and recommendations for practitioners. We hope that this work accelerates the fusion of scientific models and data and fosters a modern approach to scientific modeling.

fundamentals.title: Reconciling Discrete-Time Mixed Policies and Continuous-Time Relaxed Controls in Reinforcement Learning and Stochastic Control
fundamentals.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is currently one of the most prominent methods for optimizing dynamical systems, with breakthrough results across various fields. The framework is based on the concept of a Markov decision process (MDP), leading to a discrete-time optimal control problem. In the RL literature, such problems are typically formulated and solved using mixed policies, from which random actions are sampled at each time step. Recently, part of the optimal control community has begun investigating continuous-time versions of RL algorithms, replacing MDPs with continuous-time stochastic processes governed by relaxed controls and asserting a full analogy between the two formulations. In this work, we examine the limitations of this analogy and rigorously establish a connection between the two problems in the case where only the drift term of the continuous-time model is controlled. We prove strong convergence of the RL implementation of mixed strategies as the time discretization mesh tends to zero. We also discuss the technical challenges posed by the possible presence of control in the diffusion component of the state.

fundamentals.title: Effective gaps between singular values of non-stationary matrix products subject to non-degenerate noise
fundamentals.abstract: We study the singular values and Lyapunov exponents of non-stationary random matrix products subject to small, absolutely continuous, additive noise. Consider a fixed sequence of matrices of bounded norm. Independently perturb the matrices by additive noise distributed according to Lebesgue measure on matrices with norm less than ε ϵ . Then the gaps between the logarithms of the singular values of the random product of n n of these matrices are all of order at least ε ²n ϵ 2 n , both in expectation; and almost surely for large n n . To prove this, we develop recent work of Gorodetski and Kleptsyn [26]. That paper gives a very flexible method, based on relative entropy, for showing that a non-stationary product of matrices in SL(d,R) SL ( d , R ) has a strictly positive Lyapunov exponent. We extend their work in two ways, firstly by making the estimates quantitative in the context of absolutely continuous distributions, giving the universal estimates described above; and secondly by developing a fibered version of their methods, working on flag bundles instead of the projective space to estimate gaps between arbitrary consecutive exponents. Our methods retain much of the flexibility of those of Gorodetski and Kleptsyn, and we hope that they will find application in other related problems.

fundamentals.title: Linear scaling reveals low-dimensional structure in observable microbial dynamics
fundamentals.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
fundamentals.abstract: Microbial communities often exhibit apparently complex dynamics driven by myriad interactions among community members and with their environments. Yet, practical modeling and control are often based on a limited number of observables, raising fundamental questions: are these observed dynamics low-dimensional? If so, how does the low dimensionality enable predictions with limited information? Here, we report an emergent simplicity that the temporal dynamics of observable microbial populations can be captured by low-dimensional representations. Using variational autoencoders, we define a critical latent dimension ( E c ) that operationally quantifies the smallest latent dimension required for high-fidelity reconstruction of observable microbial dynamics under a specified criterion. Despite the complexity of unobserved background dynamics, we find E c to be drastically lower than the community’s apparent degrees of freedom. E c scales linearly with the number of observables, providing an empirical principle for determining representation complexity. This principle holds across simulations of pairwise interacting communities, consumer–resource dynamics, spatially distributed microbial patches, and plasmid transfer, experiments with engineered and environment-derived communities, and human microbiomes. Our findings establish a scaling law for microbial community dynamics and demonstrate that low-dimensional representations of observable dynamics retain information useful for selected prediction tasks without direct measurement of the complete community.

fundamentals.title: Foiling Black Hole Foils: Revealing Horizon Alternatives with Baryonic Atmospheres
fundamentals.abstract: Event horizons are a defining feature of black holes. Consequently, there have been many efforts to probe their existence in astrophysical black hole candidates, spanning 10 orders of magnitude in mass. Nevertheless, horizons remain an obstacle to unifying general relativity and quantum mechanics, most sharply presented by the information paradox. This has motivated a proliferation of horizonless alternatives (black hole foils) that avoid event horizons and are therefore presumably benign. We explore the fate of accreting material in the context of spherically symmetric horizonless compact objects in the steady state regime. We find that for typical accreting astronomical targets, foils can develop an optically thick, convectively stable baryonic atmosphere, immediately implying the creation of an emitting photosphere at modest redshift even when the surface redshift is extreme. The emergent photosphere luminosity is driven toward the accretion powered equilibrium value and is only weakly sensitive to the foil redshift. Moreover, local gas–surface interaction provides a microphysical lower bound on the effective base temperature, insulating the atmosphere from arbitrarily cold foils. The unknown properties of the foil enter only through local boundary conditions controlling baryon processing and thermal coupling at the surface, making the solutions broadly applicable to horizonless alternatives that do not invoke significant additional nonlocal interactions. Thus, under minimal assumptions (GR exterior and local surface interactions), spherically symmetric horizonless foils in accreting systems are generically observationally exposed: the absence of a thermal photosphere directly constrains or rules out broad classes of such models.

fundamentals.title: Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design
fundamentals.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.

fundamentals.title: Bright Galaxies at Cosmic Dawn: A Cloud-Scale Star Formation Model Unifying Variable SFE, IMFs, and Stochasticity
fundamentals.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
fundamentals.abstract: To investigate the origins of the high abundance of UV-bright galaxies at z > 10, we present a new semi-analytic model that bridges the gap between small-scale star formation physics and large-scale galaxy evolution by explicitly tracking discrete star-forming clouds within smoothly evolving dark matter potentials. Unlike conventional semi-analytic models, our approach naturally captures the stochasticity of star formation, allowing us to isolate how cloud properties, star formation efficiencies (SFEs), and stellar initial mass functions (IMFs) shape the star-formation burstiness of early galaxies. Clouds are drawn sequentially from a cloud mass distribution, assigned an SFE and IMF depending on cloud mass, metallicity, and redshift, and evolve under the influence of short-timescale stellar feedback. We identify three distinct star formation regimes arising from the interplay between cloud masses, densities, and feedback timescales: a stochastic, feedback-limited regime in low-mass halos with long quiescent phases; a bursty regime regulated by the cloud mass distribution; and a smooth, continuous regime in massive halos. Our fiducial model adopts a dynamic IMF, an SFE linked to cloud properties and the IMF, and massive, moderately dense clouds. Varying assumptions reveals that top-heavy IMFs and enhanced SFEs in massive clouds amplify burstiness, while altering the upper cloud mass or density normalisation is secondary. Among model ingredients, the IMF most strongly impacts the UV luminosity function (LF), while switching to a constant SFE boosts the faint end, and reducing the maximum cloud mass decreases the bright end. These results demonstrate that cloud-scale physics critically shape early galaxy UV luminosity distributions.

fundamentals.title: The commutativity problem for effective varieties of formal series, and applications
fundamentals.abstract: A formal series in noncommuting variables Σ over the rationals is a mapping Σ * → Q from the free monoid generated by Σ to the rationals. We say that it is commutative if the output does not depend on the order of the symbols in the input. The commutativity problem for a class of series takes as input a (finite presentation of) a series from the class and amounts to establishing whether it is commutative. This is a very natural, albeit nontrivial problem, which has not been considered before from an algorithmic perspective. We show that commutativity is decidable for all classes of series that constitute a so-called effective prevariety , a notion generalising Reutenauer’s varieties of formal series. For example, the class of rational series , introduced by Schützenberger in the 1960’s, is well-known to be an effective (pre)variety, and thus commutativity is decidable for it. In order to showcase the applicability of our result, we consider classes of formal series generalising the rational ones. We consider polynomial automata , shuffle automata , and infiltration automata , and we show that each of these models recognises an effective prevariety of formal series. Consequently, their commutativity problem is decidable, which is a novel result. We find it remarkable that commutativity can be decided in a uniform way for such disparate computation models. Finally, we present applications of commutativity outside the theory of formal series. We show that we can decide solvability in sequences and in power series for restricted classes of algebraic difference and differential equations, for which such problems are undecidable in full generality. Thanks to this, we can prove that the syntaxes of multivariate polynomial recursive sequences and of constructible…

fundamentals.title: Substitutional Quantification and Arithmetical Truth
fundamentals.abstract: In the mid‐20th century, there was a debate about whether the quantifiers in first‐order logic should be understood objectually or substitutionally. This debate typically focused on ontology and assumed that we could use only one of these two types of quantification. After Kripke and others influentially argued that the two kinds of quantification were logically equivalent, defenses of substitutional quantification were rare. Following Gottlieb and Field, I argue that Kripke was wrong and that substitutional consequence is language‐bound and non‐compact. While of no help with ontology, I also argue that so‐understood, substitutional quantification can be applied to help explain our grasp of a determinate notion of arithmetical truth. To argue for this, I give an account of the metasemantics of the substitutional quantifiers and prove that adding a single, very natural, mixed axiom to weak theories of arithmetic results in a categorical theory. This approach promises to explain arithmetical truth on a less controversial basis than appeals to either second‐order logic or the omega rule, thus making progress on the project of explaining our grasp of arithmetic in a naturalistically acceptable fashion.

fundamentals.title: Tidal Deformation and Strain Accumulation of Solid Compact Stars
fundamentals.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
fundamentals.abstract: The tidal deformability of compact stars encodes the equation of state of dense matter, and gravitational-wave observations such as GW170817 have begun to constrain it under the assumption of a fluid interior. Yet whether the interior of pulsar-like compact stars is fluid or solid remains largely untested, despite the distinct tidal responses the two states predict. In this work, based on the strangeon-star model, we develop a framework for modeling tidal deformation in solid compact stars. Adopting a shear modulus of μ = 1034 erg cm−3, we find a relative difference of approximately 30 % in tidal deformability between solid and fluid strangeon stars of 1.4 M⊙, corresponding to a ~10 % deviation from the universal I–Love relation. We further model the accumulation of internal strain during binary inspiral and find that it peaks near the stellar center. When the gravitational-wave frequency reaches several hundred Hz, the strain in a large fraction of the stellar volume exceeds the adopted threshold σ = 10−3, and the elastic energy stored in the threshold-exceeding region reaches ~1046 erg at these frequencies. A solid-to-fluid transition would alter the tidal response and could imprint on the waveform and phase of the emitted gravitational radiation. Combined with the precursor electromagnetic emission, these gravitational-wave signatures offer a multi-messenger avenue to test the solid nature of pulsar-like compact stars.

fundamentals.title: Improving Lives and Avoiding Harm
fundamentals.abstract: The Asymmetry in population ethics holds that creating a miserable person is morally impermissible, while not creating a happy person is morally permissible, all else being equal. Harm‐avoidance theories explain the Asymmetry by claiming that, in certain contexts, only actions resulting in harm are impermissible. Two problems threaten these theories: (i) The Problem of Improvable Life Avoidance—requiring agents to avoid creating improvable good lives—and (ii) requiring dominated options. Sophisticated harm‐avoidance theories avoid both problems. However, we show that any harm‐avoidance theory entails either (1) a worse form of The Problem of Improvable Life Avoidance, (2) a troubling form of sadism, (3) an implausibly extreme priority for avoiding a small harm for one person over greater harms for many people, or (4) spurious prohibition dilemmas. Furthermore, we argue that any reasonable theory of the Asymmetry entails at least one of (1)–(4).

fundamentals.title: A Log-Uniform Initial Magnetic Field Distribution Explains Pulsar and Magnetar Populations through Magnetic Inclination Alignment
fundamentals.journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
fundamentals.abstract: The origin of the gap in the observed magnetic field distribution between pulsars and magnetars raises a challenge to understanding these populations within a unified framework. We analytically show that the gap can be naturally explained by the alignment of the magnetic inclination angle between the magnetic and spin axes. Based on coupled evolution of spin-down and magnetic inclination angle in the plasma-filled magnetosphere, the alignment timescale follows τα∝B−2. Thus, strongly magnetized neutron stars including high-B pulsars and magnetars align more rapidly than pulsars with 1012 G, reducing their beaming fraction and thereby suppressing their observed numbers. However, magnetars are primarily identified through X-ray activity and are therefore relatively less affected by beaming. Taking into account both beaming fraction and luminosity corrections, we reconstruct the initial magnetic field distribution from the observed distribution. We show that pulsars and magnetars do not dictate intrinsically distinct initial distributions, but can instead be understood within a single continuous initial magnetic field distribution, such as a log-uniform distribution.

fundamentals.title: On the Orbital Evolution of Giant-planet Pair Embedded in a Gaseous Disk. III. Simultaneous Gas Accretion and the Final Mass Ratio
fundamentals.abstract: Recent exoplanet surveys reveal a systematic trend in the mass ratios of giant-planet pairs (>30 M ⊕ ). Although the M outer / M inner is broadly centered near unity, it exhibits a dependence on orbital separation. Compact pairs tend to have comparable masses, whereas widely separated pairs show outer-heavy configurations. To investigate the origin of this trend, we perform 2D hydrodynamic simulations that couple gas accretion and orbital migration of two giant planet embryos with initial masses of 15−30 M ⊕ . We explore the effects of disk viscosity, surface density slope, and initial mass ratio on the coupled evolution of planetary growth and migration. We find that convergent migration drives the planets to open a common gap, restructuring the gas flow. This configuration induces asymmetric accretion, in which the inner planet becomes starved as gap clearing suppresses its gas supply, while the outer planet continues to accrete from the high-density region at the outer gap edge. Consequently, the system naturally evolves toward mass-ratio convergence, and in many cases produces an inversion of the initial core-mass hierarchy. We further show that migration outcomes are highly sensitive to initial conditions. Systems with initially more massive inner cores tend to diverge, whereas steeper surface density profiles and more massive outer cores favor convergent migration and subsequent resonance capture. Overall, our results identify common-gap-driven asymmetric accretion as a unified mechanism linking orbital architecture, resonant capture, and the observed mass-ratio demographics of giant planet pairs.

fundamentals.title: A Unified Reactivity Scale Predicts Nonenzymatic Phosphoryl Transfer and Nucleophilic Catalysis in Water
fundamentals.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
fundamentals.abstract: The transfer of phosphoryl groups plays a central role in biochemical energy metabolism. Understanding how such reactions could have occurred before the emergence of enzymes is thus crucial for elucidating the chemical foundations of life. Although the factors governing the mechanisms of phosphoryl transfer in water are well understood, predicting whether a given nucleophile and phosphorylating agent will undergo productive phosphoryl transfer rather than hydrolysis remains difficult, thereby hindering the rational exploration of nonenzymatic phosphorylation reactions. Herein, we establish a quantitative reactivity scale that predicts absolute rate constants for nonenzymatic phosphoryl transfer reactions in water based on a linear free-energy relationship (LFER). Using high-throughput kinetics, we measured 11,520 phosphoryl transfer reactions for 145 unique combinations of nucleophiles and phosphorylating agents under varying reaction conditions. Mechanism-specific rate constants extracted from this data for 102 substrate pairs, together with values scraped from the literature, enabled us to parametrize an LFER that places 34 phosphorylating agents and 45 nucleophiles on a unified quantitative reactivity scale, enabling predictions across 14 orders of magnitude in reactivity. Finally, we show that the empirically derived reactivity parameters can be used to predict optimal nucleophilic catalysts by balancing the competing steps in catalytic turnover, as experimentally validated for the reaction of monoamidophosphate with pyridines. For phosphorylating agents of intermediate electrophilicity such as ATP, imidazole is predicted to be the optimal catalyst, offering a kinetic rationale for the prevalence of histidine residues in enzymatic phosphoryl transfer. fundamentals.title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
fundamentals.abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge support from the FRIC Center for Financial Frictions [Grant DNRF102]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09038 .

fundamentals.title: Bias Against Boltzmann Brains?
fundamentals.abstract: A popular indifference principle for self‐locating probability faces skeptical challenges, most notably a skeptical challenge concerning Boltzmann Brains. We examine the prospects for various views that prescribe some degree of bias in place of indifference. Although a bias view has attractive anti‐skeptical features, it turns out that bias leads to puzzles about deference to chance, reflection, and other related principles.

food.title: Impact of arsenic exposure on the gut-microbiota-liver axis in poultry
food.abstract: Arsenic (As), a priority hazardous substance widely distributed in nature, endangers poultry health and food safety. The gut‑microbiota‑liver axis forms a bidirectional regulatory network, with the intestine acting as the main absorption site and the liver as the key metabolic‑detoxification organ for As. This review summarizes arsenic‑induced toxic injuries to this axis in poultry. In the intestine, As impairs mucosal barrier function, triggers epithelial cell death via NF‑κB‑NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and causes leaky‑gut syndrome. It also disturbs gut microbiota homeostasis, lowering beneficial butyrate‑producing bacteria and impairing short‑chain‑fatty‑acid synthesis. In the liver, As disrupts energy metabolism, provokes severe oxidative stress, and triggers multiple forms of programmed cell death, including ferroptosis and PANoptosis. Gut-derived lipopolysaccharide translocates to the liver via the portal circulation, amplifying hepatic inflammation, which in turn causes altered bile acid metabolism and reduced short-chain fatty acid production, thereby triggering gut microbiota dysbiosis and forming a self-reinforcing vicious cycle. Potential interventions including probiotics, polysaccharides, selenium and vitamin E are discussed to counteract arsenic toxicity. This work provides theoretical support for arsenic risk control in poultry farming.

food.title: Interactive effects of dietary total sulfur amino acids and crude protein on productive performance in laying hens: A meta-analysis
food.abstract: Dietary total sulfur amino acids (TSAA) play essential roles in egg protein synthesis and various metabolic functions in laying hens, underscoring the importance of accurate estimation of TSAA requirements, particularly when formulating low-CP diets. A previous meta-analysis in broiler chickens revealed that optimal TSAA levels increase as dietary CP levels decrease; however, quantitative information regarding this interactive effect across different phases of the prolonged laying cycle remains limited in laying hens. Therefore, the current meta-analysis aimed to determine the interactive relationship between dietary CP and digestible TSAA levels for optimizing productive performance in laying hens across laying phases. A total of 28 studies published between 2010 and 2026 were analyzed using a mixed model with study as a random effect and observations weighted by the number of replicates. Productive performance variables included hen-d egg production (HEP), egg weight (EW), egg mass (EM), average daily feed intake (ADFI), and feed conversion ratio (FCR). The quadratic model with the product of digestible TSAA and total CP (TSAA × CP) as a single predictor, which was developed in our previous meta-analysis for broiler chickens, was fitted separately in different laying phases. Models were conservatively retained only when the intercept and regression coefficients were all significant (P < 0.05). Accordingly, models were retained for ADFI and FCR in phase 1 (early-phase), for HEP, EM, and ADFI in phase 2 (mid-phase), and for all variables in the overall dataset. However, no significant models were identified in phase 3 (late-phase), possibly due to the limited number of observations and between-study heterogeneity. food.title: Protocatechuic acid attenuates lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammatory responses in chicken macrophages by modulating the Toll-like receptor signaling pathway
food.abstract: Protocatechuic acid (PCA) possesses anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities. This study aimed to investigate the effects of PCA on lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory responses in HD11 cells and its potential mechanisms of action. The regulatory effects of PCA on LPS-induced inflammatory responses were systematically evaluated by detecting nitric oxide (NO), reactive oxygen species (ROS), inflammation-related factors, and protein expression, combined with transcriptomic sequencing analysis. The results showed that LPS stimulation significantly increased the production of NO and ROS in HD11 cells and upregulated the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interleukin-8 (IL-8). In contrast, PCA treatment reduced NO and ROS levels, downregulated the expression of IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8, and increased interleukin-10 (IL-10) expression. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that PCA modulated genes and signaling pathways associated with innate immunity and inflammatory signal transduction, including the Toll-like receptor signaling pathway. Western blot analysis further demonstrated that PCA significantly reduced LPS-induced protein expression of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) and myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88), as well as the expression of the downstream inflammatory effector proteins inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). Collectively, PCA effectively alleviated LPS-induced inflammatory responses and oxidative stress in HD11 cells, and its anti-inflammatory effects may involve the modulation of the Toll-like receptor signaling pathway and inhibition of inflammatory effector protein expression. This study provides experimental evidence for elucidating the…

food.title: Novel electron transport powers archaeal methane metabolism across varied substrates and environments
food.abstract: Methanogens are responsible for producing approximately one billion metric tons of methane each year within Earth’s anaerobic environments as a byproduct of their energy metabolism. They play a vital role in the global carbon cycle. There are three main pathways for methanogenesis: hydrogenotrophic, which uses H 2 and CO 2 to produce methane; methylotrophic, which utilizes methylated compounds like methanol and amines; and aceticlastic, which converts acetate into methane and CO 2 . Instead of substrate-level ATP production, methanogens conserve energy through a membrane-bound electron transport chain and flavin-based electron bifurcation (FBEB). Beyond the canonical modes of growth in methanogens, Methanosarcina acetivorans , a model acetotrophic methanogen, can conserve energy via direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET). Here, we review the metabolic pathways and electron transport processes involved in energy conservation during fermentative, respiratory, and DIET modes. Additionally, we discuss the role of FBEB in energy conservation in gut-associated Methanomassiliicoccus luminyensis . Finally, we discuss the potential roles of heterodisulfide reductase (Hdr) and the process of electron transfer during the reaction mechanism of electron-bifurcating HdrA2B2C2 complex in cytochrome-containing methanogens. Understanding the complex redox control mechanisms in these organisms has broader implications for sustainable energy and environmental management.

food.title: Bacterial and host cell-specific delivery of BMP, GrpE, and pMGA antigens via attenuated Salmonella confers bivalent protection against Mycoplasma gallisepticum and Salmonella Gallinarum in chickens
food.abstract: Mycoplasma gallisepticum and Salmonella Gallinarum (SG) are economically important bacterial pathogens affecting poultry production, yet no single vaccine addresses both pathogens simultaneously. We engineered a recombinant SG vaccine strain, JOL3203, based on the dual-expression plasmid pJHL270, incorporating functionally distinct prokaryotic and eukaryotic cassettes to deliver two complementary Mycoplasma gallisepticum antigens from a single immunization regimen. The bacterial cassette under the Ptrc promoter expressed a multi-epitope chimeric antigen derived from conserved B-cell, MHC class I, and MHC class II epitopes of the BMP, GrpE, pMGA1.2, and pMGA1.3 proteins. The host cell cassette under the CMV promoter expressed a domain-based fusion antigen incorporating the N-terminal 400 residues of the BMP family protein, the C-terminal 250 residues of GrpE, and immunodominant pMGA epitopes. This dual-expression strategy was designed to promote antigen presentation through both exogenous and endogenous processing pathways, thereby stimulating complementary CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T-cell responses. In silico analyses predicted high antigenicity, favorable structural quality, and strong interaction with chicken TLR2-2. Expression was confirmed by western blotting at 32 kDa in bacterial lysates and 83 kDa in infected chicken bone marrow-derived macrophages, with transcription validated by RT-PCR. JOL3203 achieved 100% survival in safety evaluations versus 83% mortality in the wild-type SG group, with minimal systemic dissemination and histopathological changes. Vaccination elicited robust Mycoplasma-specific systemic IgY, mucosal IgA, expanded CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell populations, upregulated MHC class I and II expression, and a balanced Th1/Th2 cytokine profile of IFN-γ, TNF-α, and…

food.title: Sustainable 2-keto-L-gulonic acid biosynthesis via single-strain one-step fermentation
food.abstract: L-ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is an essential antioxidant molecule that maintains normal physiological functions in humans. Currently, industrial production relies primarily on a three-strain, two-step fermentation process to produce 2-keto-L-gulonic acid (2-KLG), the direct precursor of vitamin C. 2-KLG is then converted to vitamin C through chemical lactonization. However, this process is limited by prolonged fermentation cycles, poor stability of the mixed-culture system, and complex process control. In recent years, engineered single-strain platforms capable of one-step 2-KLG biosynthesis have emerged as a promising strategy for more sustainable vitamin C production. Nevertheless, the efficiency of L-sorbose-to-2-KLG conversion in this system remains low, making it a major bottleneck to further improving 2-KLG production. This review summarizes recent advances on single-strain, one-step fermentation systems using Gluconobacter oxydans as the chassis strain. It focuses on strategies including genetic tool development, metabolic engineering, and key enzyme optimization. The review aims to provide a theoretical basis and technical reference for optimizing and industrializing green biomanufacturing systems for vitamin C.

food.title: Regulatory governance and full-scale digital transformation for prediction-based food safety management: Global trends and future perspectives
food.abstract: Background The global food safety paradigm is shifting from traditional, reactive hazard control toward proactive, predictive risk management to address increasingly complex supply chain vulnerabilities. However, current digital implementations remain fragmented, creating structural bottlenecks that hinder the transition to next-generation regulatory science. Scope and approach To our knowledge, this study provides one of the first comparative critical analyses of the HACCP-based data governance frameworks of six major jurisdictions. We compare jurisdictions in which private actors play a relatively larger role in certification and implementation ('market-led': the United States, the European Union, Canada, and Japan) with those in which public institutions play a dominant role ('state-led': South Korea and China), positioned along a governance continuum in which all systems combine public and private functions, focusing on their capacity for real-time risk prediction, public-private data integration, and global interoperability. Key findings and conclusions The market-led systems examined tend to foster food safety culture but are affected by 'Data Silos' that limit actions to retrospective tracebacks. The state-led systems examined may enhance data integrity but can create a 'Data Island' paradox due to an over-reliance on automating isolated physico-chemical Critical Control Points. To overcome these limitations, we propose a conceptual framework for Full-Scale Digital Transformation (Full DX). Converging prerequisite programs, structured food safety culture assessment (e.g., Shapley-FAHP), and intentional threat mitigations (TACCP/VACCP) into an interoperable predictive network powered by ensemble machine learning could support a more resilient regulatory…

Cultivation of halophilic archaea in shallow subsurface Martian conditions has implications for extant life on Mars
food.abstract: The present-day Martian surface is generally considered inhospitable to life because of low atmospheric pressure, intense surface radiation, global desiccation, and oxidizing chemistry, which has been increasing since the late Noachian. However, shallow Martian subsurface regions where mineralogy has shown groundwater movement may include localized hypersaline environments capable of retaining liquid water and supporting microbial metabolism. Haloferax volcanii , a model halophilic archaeon, has previously been shown to survive under low-pressure Martian conditions (24 mbar) and to grow anaerobically supported by the Mars-relevant oxyanions nitrate and perchlorate under high-salinity conditions. Here, we investigated whether H. volcanii could actively grow under a combination of environmental and chemical conditions relevant to potentially habitable shallow subsurface Martian lacustrine settings. Cultures were incubated for 160 days under anoxic, CO₂-enriched, low-pressure conditions (24 mbar) in hypersaline liquid media supplemented with nitrate or perchlorate. Growth was observed in all low-pressure treatments and was confirmed by increases in optical density and biological reduction of nitrate and perchlorate. Scanning electron microscopy revealed extensive biofilm formation in low-pressure cultures, and Raman spectroscopy demonstrated the persistence of carotenoid biosignatures after prolonged incubation under Martian conditions. Liquid loss remained below 4% across all treatments, indicating long-term stability of hypersaline brines throughout the experiment. These results demonstrate for the first time that a halophilic archaeon is capable of active growth and metabolism under a Mars-relevant combination of low pressure, high salinity, anoxia, and oxidizing…

Elevated ozone reshapes wheat root-associated microbiomes through coordinated plant responses and rhizosphere environmental filtering
food.abstract: Elevated tropospheric ozone (O 3 ) threatens crop productivity, but how O 3 -induced changes in plant responses influence root-associated microbiomes remains unclear. We investigated the responses of microbial communities inhabiting the rhizosphere and root endosphere to elevated O 3 using four cultivars grown under ambient and 1.5-fold ambient O 3 in a field-based free-air O 3 -concentration enrichment (FACE) system. Plant traits, root-released organic carbon (ROC), rhizosphere properties, extracellular enzyme activities, and bacterial and fungal communities were jointly analyzed. Elevated O 3 reduced yield and root biomass, with cultivar-dependent changes in ROC. Elevated O 3 consistently increased rhizosphere pH and altered microbial resource allocation, increasing ecoenzymatic vector length by 4.1% and decreasing vector angle by 4.6%. Bacterial communities showed a stronger response than fungal taxonomic communities, particularly in the rhizosphere. However, variation partitioning indicated that soil properties, especially pH, rather than O 3 treatment alone, provided the strongest independent explanation for bacterial community variation. Fungal communities showed limited taxonomic turnover but exhibited shifts in predicted trophic guilds, including increased pathotroph- and saprotroph-associated groups and decreased symbiotroph-containing guilds under elevated O 3 . These results demonstrate that elevated O 3 reshapes the wheat root-associated microbiome through coordinated changes in plant performance, rhizosphere environmental filtering, and microbial functional strategies, highlighting the importance of plant-mediated processes in regulating belowground responses to atmospheric change. food.title: Survey among official veterinarians on condemnation criteria for broiler carcasses with external lesions and its potential use for computer vision applications
food.abstract: Post-mortem inspection (PMI) of broiler carcasses is essential for food safety and provides insights into animal health, welfare, and meat quality. Despite uniform legislation in Europe, condemnation criteria still vary among Official Veterinarians (OVs) and countries. This study aimed to collect data regarding condemnation criteria among European OVs conducting broiler PMI and to suggest how these could be used in the compliance audits of PMI computer vision systems (CVSs). An online survey was conducted among 155 OVs in 14 European countries. Respondents assessed 11 standardized image sets depicting common external lesions on broiler carcasses across seven severity levels. They were asked to indicate the point at which each lesion should render a carcass unfit for human consumption. A consensus criterion of ≥66% was applied to define a commonly agreed severity level that requires condemnation. Open-ended responses were analyzed to explore factors affecting PMI decisions. High consensus was achieved for clearly visible and advanced lesions, with most benchmarks established at moderate to high severity levels. Greater variability was found for borderline cases, particularly cellulitis and superficial dermatitis. Qualitative analysis of open-ended questions regarding PMI identified three main themes: 1) training needs; 2) lack of harmonization and support in decision-making; 3) OVs’ public health role and implications for broiler health and welfare. The findings emphasized the role of guidelines, experience, and working conditions in condemnation decisions. The collected PMI results may serve as references for harmonized, risk-based PMI and for evaluating CVS performance against OV assessments.

food.title: Scientific criteria and guidelines for identifying, reporting and interpreting omics data – transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and lipidomics – in meat science research
food.abstract: Omics approaches offer a rapidly expanding and highly valuable means to study meat science research questions associated with on-farm and post-farm activities. To help ensure the reliability, reproducibility, and transparency of these methodologies, this paper provides practical recommendations for identifying, reporting and interpreting transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and lipidomics studies in meat research with a focus on best practices regarding the experimental designs, data analysis, and interpretation of the results. Rather than restricting methodological innovation, these guidelines aim to establish recommended scientific criteria that enhance reproducibility, facilitate the integration of independently generated omics datasets through standardized reporting, compatible metadata and transparent analytical workflows among studies submitted to Meat Science journal. Although individual technologies continue to evolve, adherence to the key principles and criteria will substantially improve the scientific soundness and long-term impact of omics generated data applied to meat science research.

food.title: Occurrence of aflatoxins, ochratoxin A, and unauthorised synthetic dyes in bulk paprika from two provinces of Türkiye: Dietary exposure and health risk assessment
food.abstract: Paprika is susceptible to contamination by naturally occurring mycotoxins and economically motivated adulteration with illegal synthetic dyes, posing potential food safety concerns. This study investigated the occurrence of four aflatoxins (AFs), ochratoxin A (OTA), and 13 unauthorised synthetic dyes in 105 unbranded bulk paprika samples collected from retail spice shops in Türkiye using validated HPLC-FLD and LC-MS/MS methods. AFB 1 was the predominant mycotoxin, detected in 70.5% of samples, whereas OTA occurred in 26.7%. Regulatory exceedances for AFB 1 were limited, and no sample exceeded the European Union maximum level for OTA. Among the prohibited dyes analysed, Sudan I and Sudan IV were detected in 5.7% and 1% of samples, respectively. Under the upper-bound scenario, deterministic margin of exposure (MOE) values were 38,531 for AFB 1 and 1,578,678 for OTA. The probabilistic assessment yielded 5th percentile MOE values of 10,535 and 377,691 for AFB 1 and OTA, respectively. All reported MOE values exceeding the reference threshold of 10,000. These findings suggest a low level of public health concern for dietary exposure to AFs and OTA through paprika consumption, while highlighting the need for continued monitoring of mycotoxins and illegal dyes to ensure food safety and product authenticity.

food.title: Using DNA barcoding to uncover mislabelling in the flake trade along the supply chain across Southeast Australia
food.abstract: Seafood is a vital global resource, providing protein and essential nutrients to millions. However, ambiguous labelling practices, including the use of umbrella terms, can obscure origin and species composition. Such practices can conceal the trade of threatened species, undermining fisheries management and consumers’ ability to make informed choices. Like other generic names used internationally (e.g., ‘cação’, ‘rock salmon’), shark meat in Australia is commonly sold under the umbrella label of flake, with no mandatory regulations defining which species can be traded under this label. To identify mislabelling and assess the mix of different products, we used DNA barcoding of the Cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) to identify the species sold as flake across the entire supply chain (from fishers and wholesalers to fresh seafood and takeaway shops) in Southeast Australia. Sampling across different seasons also allowed insights into potential links to local fisheries. Of 423 samples sequenced successfully, 144 were identified to species level, and 279 to genus level, representing a total of 16 species and 12 genera. School shark Galeorhinus galeus , a critically endangered species, made up 20 % of identifications, with other notable species including smooth hammerhead and bull shark. Species composition varied across supply chain nodes with some species such as Elephantfish Callorhinchus sp. detected only in take-away products but no other supply chain nodes, which may suggest additional sources at later distribution stages. Overall, these findings highlight that ambiguity in umbrella labelling is widespread and increases towards the consumer end of the supply chain, underscoring the need for improved transparency and labelling.

food.title: Bacterial and fungal community dynamics in black pepper (Piper nigrum) across different processing plants using culture-based and amplicon sequencing approaches
food.abstract: Black pepper (Piper nigrum) is among the most commercially relevant spices worldwide, yet its microbial ecology throughout processing remains insufficiently understood, particularly in relation to food safety. Despite being a low-water-activity product, black pepper may harbor diverse bacterial and fungal communities, including spoilage microorganisms, mycotoxigenic fungi, and foodborne pathogens. In this study, we investigated the dynamics of bacterial and fungal communities along the black pepper processing chain in three distinct processing plants. A total of 154 samples were collected from processing plants A, B, and C in São Mateus, Espírito Santo, Brazil. Culture-dependent analyses included enumeration of aerobic mesophilic bacteria, Enterobacteriaceae, lactic acid bacteria, total fungi, and xerophilic fungi; fungal isolation and identification; and Salmonella detection and confirmation. Culture-independent profiling was performed by amplicon sequencing targeting the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene and the V9 region of the 18S rRNA gene. Microbial counts increased throughout processing, indicating that post-drying operations represent critical contamination points. Fungal isolation revealed genera of hygienic and toxicological relevance, including Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium, and Cladosporium. Salmonella was detected in 14.3% of the samples, comprising nine serotypes, with the highest occurrence after drying. Amplicon sequencing identified 5 phyla and 85 genera in the fungal community, whereas for the bacterial community, 24 phyla and 475 genera were identified, with Ascomycota, Proteobacteria and Firmicutes predominating across samples. food.title: Occurrence and exposure assessment of mycotoxins in fruit-based infant foods traded in São Paulo, Brazil
food.abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the mycotoxin exposure through fruit-based infant foods and characterize the potential health risks to children up to 5 years of age. Four sampling procedures were conducted between 2024 and 2026 to collect 109 fruit-based products commercially available in Ribeirão Preto and Pirassununga, state of São Paulo, Brazil, including fruit purees ( N = 47), fruit juices ( N = 39), and fruit jellies ( N = 23). Aflatoxins (AFB 1 , AFB 2 , AFG 1 , and AFG 2 ), ochratoxin A (OTA), deoxynivalenol (DON), zearalenone (ZEN), fumonisins (FB 1 and FB 2 ) and patulin (PAT) were analyzed using ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry. Among analyzed products, 64 (58.7%) samples were contaminated by at least one mycotoxin, with FBs, ZEN, PAT, OTA and DON detected in 51.3, 17.4, 7.3, 3.7 and 1% of samples, respectively. The co-occurrence of 2-3 mycotoxins was found in 37 (33.9%) samples. The highest concentrations of DON (173.1 μg/kg) and ZEN (34.40 μg/kg) were quantified in fruit jellies, followed by OTA (14.70 μg/kg) in fruit juices, FBs (10.60 μg/kg) and PAT (9.94 μg/kg) in fruit purees. AFs were not detected in any sample analyzed. The estimated daily intake (EDI) values for DON, ZEN, FBs and PAT were below their respective tolerable daily intakes (TDIs). The middle-bound margin of exposure (MOE) for OTA was <10,000 in fruit juices, indicating potential health risks for children aged 1-5 years. The hazard quotients (HQs) for FBs, DON, ZEN, and PAT were <1 across all fruit-based infant foods, indicating no significant health concern. food.title: Biopesticide-associated Bacillus thuringiensis on retail fresh produce: occurrence, typing and implications for food-safety surveillance
food.abstract: Bacillus thuringiensis is one of the most widely used microbial biopesticides and is likely to gain further relevance in the transformation of agrifood systems. However, as a member of B. cereus sensu lato ( B. cereus s.l. ), B. thuringiensis may harbor enterotoxin genes associated with diarrheal illness, raising food-safety concerns about its presence on minimally processed fresh produce. This study aimed to generate a surveillance-oriented retail dataset on the prevalence and genetic diversity of B. thuringiensis on retail fresh produce. A total of 280 fresh produce samples, including leafy greens, vegetables, and fruits, were collected from a retail distribution center in Switzerland, and presumptive B. cereus s.l. was enumerated according to ISO 7932:2004 (limit of detection, 5 CFU/g). Presumptive B. cereus s.l. isolates were subjected to PCR-based profiling of enterotoxin genes, and B. thuringiensis -associated insecticidal toxin genes ( cry genes). Selected isolates were further characterized by Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy for clustering, and a subset was analyzed by whole-genome sequencing for high-resolution comparison with commercially used biopesticide strains. B. thuringiensis was detected in 22% of produce samples and occurred at comparable frequencies across produce categories. Isolates predominantly showed biopesticide-associated profiles, and 20 out of 22 sequenced B. thuringiensis isolates showed close genomic relatedness to commercially used biopesticide strains. These findings provide a surveillance-relevant retail baseline for biopesticide-associated B. thuringiensis on fresh produce.
